context: Marie Tharp arrived at Columbia University in 1948 «with two master’s degrees, and almost no prospect» of going to sea.

choices.text: with two master’s degrees and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees; and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees and, almost no prospect

why.A: "almost no prospect of going to sea" is not an independent clause, so comma + FANBOYS is illegal here.
why.B: Correct — two compound objects of the same preposition need no comma.
why.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on both sides.
why.D: A comma cannot separate a conjunction from what follows it.

context: Research vessels of the era «do not accept» women aboard, so Tharp worked from a drafting table.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the past-tense "worked" later in the same sentence.
why.B: Future tense is impossible for a historical fact.
why.C: Correct — matches the established past tense of the surrounding narrative.
why.D: Present progressive contradicts the historical setting.

context: For four years she plotted depth readings, «one single line at a time, one after another.»

choices.text: OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "readings."

why.A: "one single" is redundant and "one after another" repeats "at a time."
why.B: Cuts past the redundancy into the meaning: she plotted thousands of lines over four years, not one, and "at a time" is what says so.
why.C: Correct — the shortest phrasing that keeps the full meaning.
why.D: This removes the redundancy by removing the information. The sentence exists to say how slowly the plotting went, and "one line at a time" is the only place it says it.

context: «Plotting depth readings for four years, the drafting paper revealed» a mountain range running down the center of the Atlantic.

choices.text: Plotting depth readings for four years, Tharp saw emerge on her drafting paper
Plotted over four years, the depth readings on her drafting paper eventually revealed
After four years of plotting depth readings, the drafting paper showed

why.A: Dangling modifier — drafting paper cannot plot readings.
why.B: Correct — places Tharp, the actual plotter, immediately after the modifier.
why.C: Readings do not plot themselves either; the actor is still missing.
why.D: "the paper" still did not do the four years of plotting.

context: Splitting that range lengthwise was a deep V-shaped notch «— a rift valley.»

why.A: Correct — a single dash after a complete clause may introduce an appositive for emphasis.
why.B: Also defensible in isolation, but ACT will not offer two fully correct choices; the dash is what the sentence’s emphatic reveal calls for.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it.
why.D: A closing dash at the end of a sentence is not a real construction.

context: Tharp recognized what the valley implied. If the seafloor was pulling apart along that seam, then continents were moving, «a idea» then associated with Alfred Wegener.

why.A: "a" cannot precede a vowel sound.
why.B: Correct — "an" before the vowel sound in "idea."
why.C: "and" creates a nonsensical list.
why.D: "ideal" changes the meaning entirely.

context: Heezen dismissed her interpretation as "girl talk" and asked her to redraw the maps. «Therefore,» she redrew them. The rift valley appeared again.

why.A: "Therefore" implies the redrawing follows logically as a conclusion, which flattens the passage’s point.
why.B: "Nevertheless" wrongly signals that she redrew them despite being asked to.
why.C: The redrawing is not an example of anything.
why.D: Correct — the two-word sentence lands hardest with no connector, and the sequence is already clear.

context: It appeared in the North Atlantic, «in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific was another place it appeared.»

choices.text: in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and in the Pacific.
the Indian Ocean profiles, and appearing in the Pacific.
in the Indian Ocean, also the Pacific.

why.A: The third item switches to a full clause, breaking parallel structure.
why.B: Correct — three parallel prepositional phrases beginning with "in."
why.C: Mixes a noun phrase with a participial phrase.
why.D: "also the Pacific" is not parallel and creates a comma splice feel.

context: When Heezen overlaid the locations of recorded undersea earthquakes onto Tharp’s maps, the pattern of epicenters «trace» the rift valley almost exactly.

why.A: The subject is "pattern," singular, and the passage is in past tense.
why.B: Still plural, and the added pronoun is redundant.
why.C: Correct — singular subject "pattern" plus past tense to match the narrative.
why.D: Present perfect breaks the established past-tense sequence.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Heezen dismissed her interpretation as ‘girl talk.’" If deleted, the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.text: a specific detail about the professional resistance that Tharp’s discovery met at the time.
evidence that Heezen was not a competent scientist.
a transition to the paragraph about plate tectonics.
nothing of significance, since the resistance is stated elsewhere in the essay.

why.A: Correct — the quotation is the paragraph’s only concrete evidence of the dismissal Tharp faced.
why.B: The passage never evaluates Heezen’s competence; it later credits his earthquake overlay.
why.C: The sentence does not function as a transition.
why.D: No other sentence states the resistance in specific terms.

context: The maps «Tharp’s and Heezen’s» published in 1957 changed how the public pictured the planet.

why.A: Nothing is possessed here — they are the subject of "published."
why.B: Correct — a compound subject with no possession requires no apostrophe.
why.C: Adds incorrect plurals to proper names.
why.D: Introduces a possessive where none belongs.

context: Plate tectonics, the framework that now organizes all of geology, «rests substantially on» the seafloor she drew.

why.A: Correct — matches the passage’s measured, formal register.
why.B: "totally built off of" is colloquial and overstated.
why.C: "kind of" is vague and informal.
why.D: "a whole lot" clashes with the surrounding academic prose.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to write an essay explaining how one scientist’s work contributed to a major shift in scientific understanding. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it traces Tharp’s mapping from her drafting table to the acceptance of plate tectonics.
Yes, because it describes several women who worked in mid-century geology.
No, because it focuses on the obstacles Tharp faced rather than on her scientific contribution.
No, because it does not explain the mechanism of plate tectonics in detail.

why.A: Correct — the essay follows exactly that arc: her method, her discovery, and its role in tectonic theory.
why.B: Only one woman is discussed.
why.C: The obstacles are secondary; the contribution is the spine of the essay.
why.D: A detailed mechanism was never part of the stated goal.

context: They are met by a dozen volunteers with soldering irons, sewing machines, and «a rule; nobody repairs anything for you.»

choices.text: a rule: nobody repairs anything for you.
a rule, nobody repairs anything for you.
a rule nobody repairs anything for you.

why.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause before it; "...and a rule" is not one.
why.B: Correct — a colon announces the rule that follows, and the clause before it is complete.
why.C: A comma cannot join a full statement to another full statement. "Nobody repairs anything for you" could stand alone, which is what makes this a splice.
why.D: Runs two statements together with no punctuation.

context: «I starting coming two years ago» with a toaster that had stopped toasting.

choices.text: I started coming two years ago
Starting to come two years ago
Having started coming two years ago

why.A: "starting" is a participle, not a conjugated verb.
why.B: Correct — supplies a real past-tense main verb.
why.C: Leaves the sentence with no main verb at all.
why.D: Also a participial phrase, producing a fragment.

context: Ellis, «a retired elevator mechanic handed» me a screwdriver and waited.

why.A: The nonessential appositive opens with a comma but never closes.
why.B: Correct — matched pair of commas around the appositive.
why.C: A semicolon cannot close an appositive.
why.D: A dash cannot close what a comma opened.

context: Inside was not the mysterious machinery I expected, «it was a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.»

choices.text: but a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.
a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal it was.
it being a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.

why.A: Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by only a comma.
why.B: Correct — "not X but Y" is parallel and eliminates the second clause entirely.
why.C: Awkward inversion that still leaves a splice.
why.D: A participial phrase that garbles the sentence.

context: We cleaned the contact. The toaster «has worked» for another three years.

why.A: Present perfect implies the toaster is still working, but "another three years" is a closed period.
why.B: Present tense contradicts the completed span.
why.C: Correct — simple past for a finished duration.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for an event already described.

context: A toaster costs sixteen dollars, and I «had been prepared and ready to throw one away in the garbage» rather than spend twenty minutes with a screwdriver.

choices.text: had been prepared to throw one away
had been ready to throw one away in the trash

why.A: "prepared and ready" is redundant, as is "away in the garbage."
why.B: Correct — removes both redundancies without losing meaning.
why.C: Shorter, and it reports something that never happened. He was willing to throw the toaster out; the sentence goes on to say he did not.
why.D: "throw away in the trash" repeats itself.

context: The economics were not the point; the habit was. «In addition,» the Repair Café movement began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to more than two thousand locations.

why.A: "In addition" implies the new paragraph adds to the previous point, but it shifts to background information.
why.B: The movement’s founding is not a consequence of the writer’s realization.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph turns to context and needs no connector.
why.D: There is no contrast between the two ideas.

context: Its organizers keep careful records: what came in, what was fixed, what could not be. «Roughly two-thirds of items leaves» working.

choices.text: Roughly two-thirds of items is leaving
Roughly two-thirds of items has left

why.A: With fractions, the verb agrees with the object of "of" — "items" is plural.
why.B: Correct — plural verb for a plural object.
why.C: Singular and needlessly progressive.
why.D: Singular and shifts tense.

context: The remaining third leave with an explanation, «which the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.»

choices.text: which the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.
that the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.
and the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.

why.A: "which" already serves as the clause’s subject, so "it" is a redundant second subject.
why.B: Correct — removes the doubled subject.
why.C: Same doubled-subject error, and "that" would require no comma.
why.D: Leaves the clause without a clear subject.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence "He never once took the screwdriver out of my hand." Where would it most logically be placed?

choices.text: In paragraph 1, after the rule that nobody repairs anything for you.
In paragraph 2, after "Ellis... handed me a screwdriver and waited."
In paragraph 3, after the discussion of disposability.
In the final paragraph, after Ellis’s death is mentioned.

why.A: The rule is stated abstractly there; the sentence is about Ellis specifically.
why.B: Correct — it directly extends the image of Ellis handing over the screwdriver and waiting.
why.C: Paragraph 3 is about economics and habit, not about Ellis.
why.D: Placing it after his death breaks the chronology of the toaster scene.

context: The café now runs a small-appliance table «in his name, staffed from three people» he taught.

choices.text: in his name, staffed by three people
on his name, staffed by three people
in his name, staffed with three people

why.A: "staffed from" is not idiomatic English.
why.B: Correct — "in his name" and "staffed by" are both standard.
why.C: "on his name" is not idiomatic.
why.D: "staffed with" is used for equipment or categories, not for named individuals doing the staffing.

stem: Which choice best concludes the essay by tying back to its opening image of broken things?
context: Final sentence options:

choices.text: I am not a good repairer. I am a patient one, which he told me is most of the job.
Repair Cafés can be found in over two thousand locations worldwide.
Ellis was seventy-eight when he died, and he had worked on elevators for forty years.
Everyone should learn to use a screwdriver at some point in their life.

why.A: Correct — returns to the essay’s personal thread and to Ellis’s lesson about the nature of repair.
why.B: A statistic already given, with no connection to the closing image.
why.C: Biographical detail that does not resolve the essay’s idea.
why.D: A generic moral that abandons the specific voice of the piece.

context: The trees grew a hundred feet tall «and eight feet across, produced reliable annual nut crops, and yielded» straight, rot-resistant timber.

choices.text: and eight feet across produced reliable annual nut crops and yielded
and eight feet across; produced reliable annual nut crops; and yielded
and eight feet across, produced reliable annual nut crops and, yielded

why.A: Correct — three parallel verbs in a series, properly separated by commas.
why.B: Removing the commas fuses the list into unreadable prose.
why.C: Semicolons are only for list items that themselves contain commas.
why.D: Places a comma between the conjunction and its verb.

context: «Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.» Asian chestnuts had coevolved with it and tolerated it.

choices.text: The cause was Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.
Cryphonectria parasitica being a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.
Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus, having arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.

why.A: A noun followed by an appositive with no main verb is a fragment.
why.B: Correct — supplies subject and verb ("The cause was").
why.C: "being" is not a conjugated main verb.
why.D: Still a fragment, now with an extra dangling appositive.

context: Asian chestnuts had coevolved with the fungus and tolerated it. American chestnuts had not. «This» moved outward at roughly twenty-four miles a year.

why.A: "This" has no clear antecedent — it could point to the fungus, the tolerance, or the whole situation.
why.B: Plural and equally vague.
why.C: Correct — naming the noun removes the ambiguity.
why.D: "It" could refer to the fungus or to either chestnut species.

context: Within forty years an estimated four billion trees «are» dead.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the completed historical span.
why.B: Correct — simple past matches the narrative of the blight’s spread.
why.C: Present perfect suggests the dying continues into the present.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for a completed event.

context: Most Americans alive today have never seen a mature chestnut. The species, «therefore,» is not extinct.

why.A: Extinction does not follow from people not having seen the tree.
why.B: Correct — signals the contrast between apparent total loss and continued survival.
why.C: Survival is not an addition to the loss; it opposes it.
why.D: The survival is not an example of the loss.

context: Millions of these stump sprouts «persists» across the Appalachians.

why.A: "Millions" is plural, so the singular verb is wrong.
why.B: Correct — plural subject takes a plural verb.
why.C: Singular and shifts the tense unnecessarily.
why.D: Singular and needlessly progressive.

context: «Girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, an estimated four billion trees were killed by the blight.»

choices.text: Girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, the blight killed an estimated four billion trees.
Girdled trunks and cut nutrient flow killed an estimated four billion trees.
An estimated four billion trees, girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, died across the range.

why.A: Dangling modifier — the trees did not girdle themselves.
why.B: Correct — places "the blight," which does the girdling, right after the modifier.
why.C: Changes the meaning and drops the blight as the agent.
why.D: Attaches the modifier to the trees, repeating the original error.

context: Breeders cross American chestnuts with Chinese varieties and then «backcrossing the hybrids» repeatedly toward American characteristics.

why.A: "cross... and backcrossing" mixes a conjugated verb with a participle.
why.B: Correct — both verbs share the subject "Breeders" in the same form.
why.C: An infinitive does not parallel "cross."
why.D: Adding a subject creates a comma splice with no conjunction adjustment.

stem: The writer is considering adding: "Chestnut wood was also prized by furniture makers in the nineteenth century." Should the sentence be added to the final paragraph?

choices.text: Yes, because it explains why the chestnut was economically valuable.
Yes, because it provides a transition to the restoration efforts.
No, because the final paragraph concerns restoration research, not the tree’s historical uses.
No, because the essay has already stated that chestnut timber was rot-resistant and durable.

why.A: True but irrelevant to the paragraph’s subject.
why.B: It does not transition to anything; it interrupts.
why.C: Correct — identifies the actual mismatch between the detail and the paragraph’s focus.
why.D: The essay mentions rot resistance but not furniture makers, so the stated reason is inaccurate.

context: None has yet produced a tree that can be planted at scale, and «due to the fact that» any restored forest will take a century to grow, patience is required.

choices.text: on account of the fact that

why.A: "due to the fact that" is a five-word way of saying one word.
why.B: Correct — the concise standard form.
why.C: Six words where one would do. Length is the fault, and this is longer than the original.
why.D: "Owing to the fact that" is the same padding with a different opening word.

context: A third group works with hypovirulence, a virus that weakens the «fungus’s own ability» to kill tissue.

why.A: Correct — singular noun ending in -s takes apostrophe + s for possession.
why.B: A plural with no apostrophe cannot show possession.
why.C: No possessive marker at all.
why.D: Shifts to plural, contradicting the single fungus under discussion.

stem: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to explain both the cause of a species’ collapse and current efforts to reverse it. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it identifies the fungus and describes three restoration approaches.
Yes, because it lists every tree species affected by an imported pathogen anywhere.
No, because it does not explain how the fungus reached North America.
No, because it focuses only on the historical importance of the chestnut.

why.A: Correct — the essay names the pathogen, traces the collapse, and details breeding, transgenic, and hypovirulence work.
why.B: Only one species is discussed.
why.C: The essay does state it arrived on imported Japanese stock.
why.D: Historical importance occupies one paragraph of five.

context: Other researchers have inserted «a wheat gene, that neutralizes the acid, the fungus uses» to kill tissue.

choices.text: a wheat gene that neutralizes the acid the fungus uses
a wheat gene, that neutralizes the acid the fungus uses
a wheat gene that neutralizes the acid, the fungus uses

why.A: Both commas are illegal — one precedes "that," the other splits the noun from its modifying clause.
why.B: Correct — essential clauses take no commas at all.
why.C: A comma before "that" is essentially always wrong.
why.D: Separates "acid" from the clause identifying it.

context: My grandmother’s bakery opened at six, «which meant: her day began at one.»

choices.text: which meant her day began at one.
which meant; her day began at one.
which meant, that her day began at one.

why.A: A colon cannot follow an incomplete clause like "which meant."
why.B: Correct — no punctuation is needed inside the relative clause.
why.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause before it.
why.D: A comma before "that" is wrong and "that" is unnecessary here.

context: My mother, out of options and patience, sent «I» to Queens for eight weeks.

why.A: "I" is a subject pronoun; this is the object of "sent."
why.B: Correct — object pronoun receiving the action.
why.C: Reflexives require the subject and object to be the same person.
why.D: "mine" is possessive and ungrammatical here.

context: She moved between the mixer, the proofing cabinet, and the oven «in a sequence, that had no visible logic.»

choices.text: in a sequence that had no visible logic.
in a sequence; that had no visible logic.
in a sequence — that had no visible logic.

why.A: A comma before "that" is wrong; the clause is essential.
why.B: Correct — no punctuation before an essential relative clause.
why.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence after it.
why.D: A dash also wrongly separates the noun from its essential modifier.

context: At three in the morning she «hands» me a bench scraper and pointed at a mound of dough.

why.A: Present tense conflicts with "pointed" in the same compound predicate.
why.B: Correct — both verbs must be past tense.
why.C: Present perfect breaks parallel structure with "pointed."
why.D: Present progressive clashes with the past-tense narrative.

context: I ruined the first four batches, «the rolls came out dense, or flat, or fused into a single continental mass.»

which came out dense, or flat, or fused into a single continental mass.
and the rolls came out dense, or flat, or fused into a single continental mass.

why.A: Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by a comma alone.
why.B: Turns the second half into a participial phrase, which reads awkwardly and loses the parallel.
why.C: "which" would have to refer to "batches," creating a vague reference.
why.D: Correct — comma + FANBOYS legally joins the two independent clauses.

context: She did not scold me, «which was somehow worse.»

choices.text: a silence that was somehow worse.

why.A: "which" vaguely refers to the entire preceding idea rather than a specific noun.
why.B: Correct — names the referent, eliminating the vague pronoun.
why.C: "this" is equally vague and creates a comma splice.
why.D: "it" still lacks a clear antecedent.

context: By the fourth week I could shape a roll that held its form. «By the sixth, understanding why she touched the dough constantly.»

choices.text: By the sixth I understood why she touched the dough constantly.
By the sixth, an understanding of why she touched the dough constantly.
The sixth week, understanding why she touched the dough constantly.

why.A: Fragment — no conjugated verb.
why.B: Correct — parallels the preceding sentence’s structure with a real main verb.
why.C: A noun phrase, still a fragment.
why.D: Also a fragment with no subject-verb pair.

context: There was no recipe «in the sense that I had previously believed in recipes in the past.»

choices.text: in the sense I had believed in recipes.
OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "recipe."

why.A: "previously" and "in the past" say the same thing twice.
why.B: Correct — removes the redundancy while keeping the meaning.

context: There «was only conditions, and adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembered in her hands.»

choices.text: were only conditions, and adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembered in her hands.
is only conditions, and adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembered in her hands.
was only conditions, adjustments, and forty years of adjustments remembering in her hands.

why.A: In "there ___" constructions the subject follows the verb; "conditions... adjustments" is plural.
why.B: Correct — plural verb agreeing with the compound plural subject, in past tense.
why.C: Correct number but wrong tense for the narrative.
why.D: Keeps the singular verb and misuses "remembering."

context: The rolls came out even and golden. «Similarly,» she looked at the tray for a long moment.

why.A: "Similarly" implies a comparison that does not exist between the rolls and her looking.
why.B: Correct — the relationship is simple sequence.
why.C: There is no contrast to signal.
why.D: Grammatical, but the two sentences then sit side by side with nothing to say the second follows the first. "Then" is what makes the pause a consequence of the rolls coming out right.

stem: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "I had never opened an appliance before" would best be placed in this essay:

choices.text: in paragraph 1, after the mention of the eight weeks in Queens.
nowhere — it belongs to a different essay entirely.
in the final paragraph, before the grandmother sits on the crate.
in paragraph 2, after she hands the narrator the bench scraper.

why.A: The detail concerns appliances, not baking, and paragraph 1 sets up the summer.

stem: The final paragraph is primarily intended to:

reinterpret a gesture the narrator had previously misunderstood.
explain the technical process of running a bakery oven.
describe the narrator’s decision to become a baker.

context: Forty years of adjustments were remembered in «her’s hands.»

why.B: "hers" stands alone and cannot modify a noun.
why.C: Correct — "her" is the possessive adjective form.

context: She was reading the humidity, which changed the flour, which «in turn changed on everything.»

why.B: Correct — "changed everything" takes a direct object with no preposition.
why.C: "changed for" alters the meaning to substitution.

context: The tower is a fourteen-foot-square room on stilts, «ringed by windows furnished with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.»

ringed by windows; furnished with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.
ringed by windows and furnished, with a bed, a stove, and an Osborne Firefinder.

why.A: Two parallel participial phrases need a comma between them.
why.B: Correct — separates the two descriptive phrases modifying "room."
why.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it.

context: an Osborne Firefinder «— a rotating brass sighting device, essentially unchanged since 1915,» that lets an observer report a bearing.

choices.text: — a rotating brass sighting device, essentially unchanged since 1915 —
, a rotating brass sighting device, essentially unchanged since 1915 —
a rotating brass sighting device essentially unchanged since 1915

why.A: The description opens with a dash and closes with a comma. The sentence then has no mark telling the reader where the interruption ended and the main clause resumed.

why.C: Mixes an opening comma with a closing dash.
why.D: Removes all punctuation, fusing the appositive into the sentence.

context: She «is hired» in 1974, when the Forest Service still staffed more than five thousand towers.

why.A: Present tense contradicts the 1974 date.
why.B: Correct — simple past matches "staffed" in the same sentence.
why.C: Present perfect implies an ongoing or unspecified time.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for a past event.

context: By the time she retired, fewer than three hundred «towers remains» active.

why.A: "towers" is plural and the passage is in past tense.
why.B: Correct — plural subject with past-tense verb.
why.C: "has remained" is singular and present perfect, and the subject is plural and the passage past.
why.D: "three hundred tower" is ungrammatical.

context: Satellites detect heat signatures from orbit; aircraft fly grid patterns; «lightning-strike sensors are triangulating ground contacts» within minutes.

the triangulation of ground contacts by lightning-strike sensors

why.A: Shifts to progressive while the other two clauses use simple present.
why.B: Correct — matches "detect" and "fly" in form.
why.C: Shifts to passive voice, breaking the parallel.
why.D: A noun phrase, producing a fragment.

context: The technology is genuinely better at finding fires that have already grown. «Similarly,» what the technology is not better at is seeing the fire that has not started yet.

why.A: "Similarly" signals likeness where the sentence draws a contrast.
why.B: The limitation is not a consequence of the strength.
why.C: Correct — the sentence’s own structure ("What the technology is not better at") already carries the contrast.
why.D: The limitation is not an example of the strength.

context: She knew which drainages held humidity into August and which slopes cured early, and «this» let her predict ignitions.

why.A: "this" vaguely refers to the whole preceding clause.
why.B: "That" points at the whole preceding clause exactly as "this" does, so the referent is still unnamed.
why.C: Correct — naming the referent removes the ambiguity.

why.B: The sentence needs to concede the lot's low material output while pivoting to a different kind of value it does have. "Still" is the concessive pivot that does exactly that; the other options imply a causal or comparative relationship that isn't present.
why.A: Implies the lot's other value is a result of its low vegetable yield, a causal link the sentence doesn't support.
why.C: The second sentence isn't an example of the low yield discussed in the first sentence — it introduces a separate kind of value entirely.
why.D: The sentence introduces something different from vegetable yield (social and communal value), not something comparable to it.

context: Which choice, placed at [2], best signals the contrast between the collection's beginning and its present size?

why.A: The sentence before describes a single donated wheelbarrow; the sentence at [2] describes more than nine hundred items. The relationship is one of time and contrast, and 'Today' marks both without overstating the logical connection.
why.B: Signals an illustration, but nine hundred items is not an example of one wheelbarrow.
why.C: Signals likeness, which is the opposite of the contrast the two sentences set up.
why.D: Signals restatement, but the second sentence adds new information rather than rephrasing the first.

context: The entries were «spare: wind» direction, cloud cover, the hour the lamp was lit, and whatever else struck her as worth recording.

why.A: Correct — "The entries were spare" is a complete sentence, and a colon is the right mark to introduce the list that explains it.
why.B: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and the list of items that follows is not one.
why.C: A comma is too weak to announce a list, and here it would read as though "wind direction" were simply one more thing the entries were.
why.D: A list following a colon does not begin with a capital letter unless it starts an independent clause.

context: Pell had no training as a «scientist, she had been hired» in 1889 because her husband held the post.

why.A: This is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by a comma alone.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon properly joins two closely related independent clauses.
why.C: Removing the comma produces a fused sentence, which is worse than the splice.
why.D: The tense change does nothing to fix the splice, and "had been hiring" wrongly suggests Pell was doing the hiring.

context: The almanac «— a ledger she kept for fifty-one years,» sat in a county archive for most of a century.

choices.text: — a ledger she kept for fifty-one years —
, a ledger she kept for fifty-one years —
- a ledger she kept for fifty-one years -

why.A: A dash opens the description and a comma closes it. An interrupter has to be bracketed by two of the same mark, whichever mark is chosen.
why.B: Correct — both ends of the description now carry a dash, so "The almanac sat in a county archive" reads straight through with the ledger held aside.
why.C: Same mismatch in the other direction: a comma cannot be closed by a dash.
why.D: These are hyphens, not dashes. A hyphen joins parts of a word; it cannot set off a phrase.

context: Alcantara «— who had come looking for shipping records,» spent two years transcribing the almanac.

choices.text: — who had come looking for shipping records —
, who had come looking for shipping records —
who had come looking for shipping records

why.A: The interrupter opens with a dash and closes with a comma, so the pair does not match.
why.B: Correct — matching dashes on both sides cleanly enclose the aside.
why.C: This reverses the same mismatch rather than fixing it.
why.D: With no punctuation at all, the clause runs into the main verb and the sentence loses its subject boundary.

context: «Looking for shipping records, the ledger was opened» instead.

choices.text: Looking for shipping records, Alcantara opened the ledger
The ledger, looking for shipping records, was opened
Looking for shipping records, the opening of the ledger happened

why.A: This dangles the modifier: as written, the ledger is doing the looking.
why.B: Correct — the person who was looking, Alcantara, now follows the modifier directly.
why.C: Moving the phrase inside the sentence still attaches it to the ledger.
why.D: An event cannot look for records either, and the phrasing is needlessly heavy.

context: Every evening at sunset she «only wrote a single line» in the ledger.

why.A: Before the verb, "only" limits the act of writing — as though writing were the single thing she did that evening — rather than limiting how much she wrote.
why.B: Correct — "only" belongs directly before "a single line," the amount it actually restricts.
why.C: Trailing "only" attaches loosely and could modify the ledger instead of the line.
why.D: This inverts the subject and verb for no reason and reads as though the line did the writing.

context: The inspectors found the brass polished, the wicks trimmed, and «the ledger was current».

why.A: The first two items are noun-plus-participle phrases; a full clause breaks the pattern.
why.B: Correct — "the ledger current" matches "the brass polished" and "the wicks trimmed" exactly.
why.C: Adding "that" turns the third item into a subordinate clause, which the first two are not.
why.D: "Being" adds a word the other two items do not have, so the three no longer match.

context: Pell's almanac recorded when the ice broke, when the ducks arrived, and «the running of the herring».

why.A: A noun phrase cannot sit in a series whose other members are "when" clauses.
why.B: Correct — "when the herring ran" matches the two clauses before it in both structure and tense.
why.C: This is a noun phrase with a relative clause, still not parallel to "when the ice broke."
why.D: "How" changes the meaning from timing to manner, and the progressive tense breaks the pattern too.

context: That trend has since been «corroborated with» three other regional records.

why.A: "Corroborated with" names an instrument rather than a source. The records are what do the corroborating.
why.B: Correct — evidence is corroborated by whatever supplies the confirmation, which is the idiom English settled on.
why.C: "From" would name an origin, which is not the relationship between evidence and the claim it supports.
why.D: "Through" implies a route or a means, not the agent doing the corroborating.

context: In 1994 a graduate student named Teodoro Alcantara, «looking for» shipping records, opened it instead.

why.A: Correct — "look for" means to search for something, which is what he was doing in the archive.
why.B: "Look after" means to care for or supervise, which makes no sense applied to records he had not found.
why.C: "Look into" means to investigate a matter, but the sentence needs the sense of searching for a specific item.
why.D: "Look at" means to direct your eyes toward something already in front of you.

context: Pell's ledger reached back into the «1880s, it was» continuous.

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma make a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — adding the coordinating conjunction "and" makes the comma legal.
why.C: With no punctuation the two sentences fuse, which is a worse version of the same error.
why.D: "Being" creates a dangling fragment rather than joining the clauses.

context: Every evening Pell «recorded: wind» direction, cloud cover, and the hour the lamp was lit.

why.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence. "Every evening Pell recorded" is missing its object, so the colon cuts the verb off from what it acts on.
why.B: Correct — with no mark at all, the verb runs straight into its list of objects, which is what the grammar requires.
why.C: A comma between a verb and its direct object is not allowed either.
why.D: A semicolon has the same problem as the colon, and it additionally requires a full sentence on both sides.

context: Two things made the almanac «valuable: its» daily entries and its unbroken span.

why.A: Correct — a complete sentence precedes the colon, and the two noun phrases after it name the "two things" just promised.
why.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on the right, but "its daily entries and its unbroken span" is only a phrase.
why.C: A comma cannot introduce an explanatory list after a complete statement like this one.
why.D: The material after a colon is capitalized only when it is itself a full sentence.

context: Three regional records «— one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line,» have since corroborated the trend.

choices.text: , one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line,
— one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line —
one from a lightship, one from a cannery, and one from a ferry line

why.A: The list opens behind a dash and closes with a comma, which leaves the reader unable to see where the list stops and the verb picks up.
why.B: Commas here compete with the three commas inside the list, leaving the reader unsure where the aside ends.
why.C: Correct — a matched pair of dashes. Dashes rather than commas, because the list being set off has commas inside it already.
why.D: With no punctuation the list collides with the main verb, and the sentence reads as though the records themselves were the three items.

context: The city expected complaints about three «things: the» view, the lighting, and the price.

why.A: Correct — a complete sentence precedes the colon, and the three items after it deliver exactly what the sentence promised.
why.B: A semicolon requires a complete sentence after it, and a list of noun phrases is not one.
why.C: A comma turns the sentence into a four-item list, so "three things" becomes one of the things.
why.D: Material after a colon is capitalized only when it is itself a complete sentence.

context: Each synchronized step «feeds: the» motion that produced it, and the sway grows.

why.A: A colon can only follow a complete sentence, and "Each synchronized step feeds" is missing the object of the verb.
why.B: Correct — nothing should separate a verb from its direct object.
why.C: A comma between a verb and its object is not allowed either.
why.D: A semicolon has the same defect as the colon, and it also demands a full sentence on each side.

context: The answer depended on a single «measurement: the» number of walkers on the deck at once.

why.A: Correct — the colon follows a complete sentence and introduces the phrase that identifies the measurement.
why.B: What follows is a noun phrase, not an independent clause, so a semicolon cannot join it.
why.C: A period leaves "The number of walkers on the deck at once" standing alone as a fragment.
why.D: Capitalizing after a colon is reserved for material that is a complete sentence.

context: The bridge still «flexes, it no longer» amplifies.

why.A: Two complete sentences joined by a comma alone form a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon is the right mark for two short, sharply contrasted independent clauses.
why.C: With no punctuation the clauses fuse into a run-on.
why.D: "No more" does not fix the splice, and it is the wrong idiom for describing an ongoing state.

context: Ordinarily those pushes are «scattered, they» cancel.

why.A: This is a comma splice: a comma cannot by itself join two independent clauses.
why.B: Correct — a comma plus the coordinating conjunction "and" is a standard way to join them.
why.C: Dropping the comma produces a fused sentence rather than repairing the splice.
why.D: A semicolon already does the joining, so adding "and" after it is redundant and incorrect.

context: The knowledge «existed, the codes» had simply not caught up to it.

why.A: Both halves are complete sentences, so a comma alone splices them.
why.B: Correct — the semicolon joins two independent clauses whose contrast is the point of the sentence.
why.C: Removing the comma fuses the two sentences together.
why.D: The extra comma sets off "the codes" as though it were an interrupter, leaving the second clause without a subject.

context: Adding stiffness would have raised the bridge's natural frequency, but it would also «have cost» more than the bridge did.

why.A: Correct — "would also have cost" matches the "would have raised" construction in the first half of the sentence.
why.B: The past participle of "cost" is "cost"; "costed" is used only for the separate sense of estimating a price.
why.C: Dropping "have" breaks the match with "would have raised" and changes the time frame.
why.D: The progressive form does not pair with "would also" here and abandons the parallel structure entirely.

context: The dampers absorb energy rather than «resisting force».

why.A: "Rather than" joins two comparable elements, and an -ing form does not match the plain verb "absorb."
why.B: Correct — "absorb energy rather than resist force" puts both verbs in the same form.
why.C: The infinitive does not match "absorb" either, and it adds a word the first half lacks.
why.D: Adding a subject turns the second half into a clause, which cannot be paired with a bare verb phrase.

context: «Gripping the rails, the movement grew» until the crossing ended.

choices.text: Gripping the rails, pedestrians felt the movement grow
The movement, gripping the rails, grew
Gripping the rails, the growth of the movement continued

why.A: As written the movement is doing the gripping, which is impossible.
why.B: Correct — the pedestrians are the ones gripping, so naming them right after the modifier fixes the attachment.
why.C: Moving the phrase into the middle still attaches it to "the movement."
why.D: An abstract growth cannot grip a rail either, so the modifier still dangles.

context: «Tuned to the frequency the crowd had found, the city installed» dampers beneath the deck.

choices.text: Tuned to the frequency the crowd had found, the dampers were installed
The city, tuned to the frequency the crowd had found, installed
Tuning to the frequency the crowd had found, the city installed

why.A: The opening phrase describes whatever noun follows it, so this says the city was tuned to a frequency.
why.B: Correct — the dampers are what was tuned, so they belong directly after the modifier.
why.C: Relocating the phrase still attaches it to "the city."
why.D: Changing the participle to "tuning" makes the city perform the tuning of itself, which is still wrong.

context: A person walking pushes sideways a little «with» every step.

why.A: Correct — "with every step" is the standard phrasing for something that accompanies each repetition of an action.
why.B: "By every step" would name a means, as though the steps caused the push from outside.
why.C: "In every step" would place the push inside the step rather than alongside it.
why.D: "From every step" names a source and does not fit the repeated-action sense the sentence needs.

context: The bridge was strong enough «for holding» many times the crowd standing on it that morning.

why.A: "Strong enough" takes an infinitive, not a gerund phrase: enough to do something, never enough for doing it.
why.B: Correct — "strong enough to hold" is the idiom, and the infinitive is what "enough" is looking for.
why.C: "To" here is part of the infinitive, so it must be followed by the base verb "hold," not "holding."
why.D: "In holding" describes a circumstance and does not complete the "strong enough" construction.

context: Pedestrian lock-in «depends of» the number of walkers rather than their weight.

why.A: Nothing depends "of" anything in English; the verb has never taken that preposition.
why.B: Correct — the verb is fixed to "on", whatever the thing being depended upon happens to be.
why.C: "Depends from" appears only in the unrelated architectural sense of hanging from something.
why.D: "Depends in" is not an accepted pairing for this verb.

context: What it got instead were «complaints about» the walking.

why.A: Correct — a complaint is about its subject; that is the standard pairing.
why.B: "Complaints on" suggests a report delivered on a topic rather than an objection to it.
why.C: "Complaints for" would name a reason or a recipient, not the thing objected to.
why.D: "Complaints to" names the person receiving the complaint, not its subject.

context: The «keepers logbooks» went back to the 1880s, four entries a day in a hand that changed as the decades passed.

why.A: The books belong to the keepers, and a possessive has to be marked.
why.B: Singular possessive, but the passage describes generations of keepers, not one.
why.C: Correct — a plural noun already ending in s takes the apostrophe after the s.
why.D: Marks the thing owned instead of the owner.

context: «Its» beam never changed; what changed was that nobody was there to watch it.

why.A: Correct — the possessive of "it" is the one possessive in English that takes no apostrophe.
why.B: Contracts "it is," which turns the opening into "it is beam."
why.C: Not a form English has; "it" has no plural possessive.
why.D: Plural, but the beam belongs to a single lamp.

context: She left at fifty-one with two suitcases and a barometer. «Which she had been told she could keep.»

choices.text: which she had been told she could keep.
She had been told she could keep it.
Having been told she could keep it.

why.A: A relative clause standing alone is a fragment; there is no main verb governing it.
why.B: Lowercasing does not help while the period before it still cuts the clause off from its noun.
why.C: Correct — it becomes an independent clause with its own subject and verb.
why.D: A participial phrase, which is still not a sentence.

context: «Recorded four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.»

choices.text: The weather was recorded four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.
Recorded four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s, by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.
Recording it four times a day, every day, in books going back to the 1880s by keepers who had no particular choice but to be looking.

why.A: A long participial phrase is still a phrase; nothing here is being said about anything.
why.B: Correct — supplying a subject and a finite verb turns the phrase into a sentence.
why.C: Adds a comma to a fragment, which leaves it a fragment.
why.D: Swaps one participle for another without ever reaching a main verb.

context: Keepers logged the things nobody had asked them to log «— fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets,» and they logged them four times a day.

, fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets —
; fog banks, bird strikes, the first gannets;

why.A: The interruption opens with a dash and closes with a comma; a pair has to match.
why.B: Correct — an interrupter that contains its own commas is set off by a matching pair of dashes.
why.C: Still mismatched, with the dash and the comma simply swapped.
why.D: Semicolons join independent clauses, and this is a list rather than a clause.

why.B: Correct — dashes are the one pair strong enough to enclose a list that is itself comma-separated.
why.C: Opens with a dash and closes with a comma, so the reader never learns where the interruption ended.
why.D: A colon cannot close anything, and nothing before it announces a list.

context: The job came down to one thing «, maintenance:» brass, glass, damp, and rust.

why.A: Announces the list with a comma and then punctuates the apposition with a colon, which is backwards.
why.B: Correct — a colon introduces the word the sentence has been building toward, and a dash then opens the list that expands it.
why.C: Two colons in one sentence leave the reader unsure which one is doing the announcing.
why.D: Sets the word off as an aside and leaves the list with nothing to attach to.

context: The radio link reports exactly one «fact; lamp» on or lamp off, and it reports that fact perfectly.

why.A: "Lamp on or lamp off" is the fact being named rather than a second statement about it, so it cannot sit on the far side of a semicolon.
why.B: Correct — the colon names the one fact the link reports, which is what the first half of the sentence has promised.
why.C: A comma is too weak to carry the announcement the sentence has set up.
why.D: Runs the announcement into its own answer with no punctuation at all.

context: «The light never went out, the keeper simply stopped being there to watch it.»

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone is a splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon joins two complete clauses that belong in one sentence.
why.C: Removing the comma makes a fused sentence, which is worse than the splice.
why.D: The conjunction would fix it, but the comma after it cuts the second clause off from its own joint.

context: «She is not sentimental about the rock, however, she still writes the pressure down every morning.»

why.B: Correct — a semicolon carries the joint and the following comma marks the adverb as an aside.
why.C: Stripping the punctuation fuses the two clauses outright.
why.D: Moves the splice rather than repairing it; a comma is still the only thing between two sentences.

context: The automated lamp switched itself on with more «preciseness» than any keeper had ever managed.

why.A: A real word, but a clumsy one where the ordinary noun exists and is shorter.
why.B: Correct — the standard noun, and the one a reader expects after "more."
why.C: Inflates the phrase and then leaves the trailing words doing no work.
why.D: An adjective where the comparison needs a noun.

context: None of it was science exactly; it was «attention», recorded by someone who had no particular choice but to be looking.

why.A: Correct — the essay's point is that the keepers were looking rather than measuring, and this is the only choice that says so.
why.B: Carries a sense of watching people under suspicion, which the passage never suggests.
why.C: Curiosity is voluntary, and the sentence insists the looking was not.

context: The «seeds» survival depended on how little moisture the cave allowed it to keep.

Then, setting it in a pot of ordinary soil.

context: «A library with the lights off, whose single design goal is that nothing inside it should ever happen.»
