why.C: "Sentimental for" reverses the sense toward longing for something rather than having feelings about it.
why.D: "Sentimental with" would describe how she treats a person, not what she feels about a situation.

context: For the last nine years she «is» the only person on Ellis Street who still letters by hand.

why.A: "For the last nine years" runs from the past into the present, and the present perfect is the tense built for that span.
why.B: The simple present describes now only, and cannot carry a nine-year stretch.
why.C: The simple past would place the whole span in a finished period and imply she no longer is.
why.D: The future contradicts a period that has already elapsed.

context: The vocabulary of the trade, along with the tools it names, «have» mostly gone out of the language.

why.A: "Along with" does not create a compound subject. The subject is still the singular "vocabulary".
why.B: The plural verb is agreeing with "tools", which sits inside a parenthetical phrase rather than in the subject.
why.C: "Were" is plural and also shifts the sentence out of the perfect that "gone" requires.
why.D: "Are" is plural, and "are gone out" is not an English construction.

context: She spends her weekdays «setting type on a screen and her Saturdays to work in the shop».

choices.text: setting type on a screen and her Saturdays working in the shop
to set type on a screen and her Saturdays working in the shop
setting type on a screen and her Saturdays she works in the shop

why.A: "Spends X doing, and Y doing" — both halves need the same gerund form for the shared verb to reach them.
why.B: "To work" is an infinitive where the first half used a gerund, so the two halves no longer match.
why.C: Fixes the second half and breaks the first, which leaves the sentence exactly as unparallel.
why.D: Turns the second half into a clause with its own subject and verb, which "spends" can no longer govern.

context: «Spaced by eye against the actual wall, a printer cannot make these decisions.»

choices.text: Spaced by eye against the actual wall, the letters reflect decisions a printer cannot make.
Spacing by eye against the actual wall, a printer cannot make these decisions.
Spaced by eye against the actual wall, these decisions cannot be made by a printer.

why.A: The letters are what gets spaced by eye, so the letters must follow the opening phrase.
why.B: As written, the printer is the thing spaced by eye against the wall.
why.C: "Spacing" makes the printer the one doing the spacing, which is precisely what the passage denies it can do.
why.D: Now the decisions are what was spaced by eye, which is no closer to the meaning.

context: «The reason that she charges more is because» the work takes longer and no one else can do it.

choices.text: The reason for her charging more is on account of

why.A: Four words instead of seven, and the cause is stated once rather than twice.
why.B: "The reason … is because" says the causal relationship twice over, once in "reason" and again in "because".
why.C: Swaps "because" for "on account of" and keeps the doubled cause, while adding a nominalization.
why.D: Concise to the point of breaking: "She charges more the work takes longer" joins two statements with no connective between them.

context: The trade has a vocabulary of its own«;» the layout, the pounce pattern, the fitch and the quill.

why.A: What follows is four nouns, and a semicolon cannot stand between a full clause and a bare list of nouns.
why.B: Correct — the clause announces a vocabulary and the colon opens the list of words that make it up.
why.C: A comma makes "the layout" look like the first of several things the trade has, rather than the first item of the vocabulary.
why.D: "Namely" does not change what a semicolon needs on its right.

context: She has taught the words to four apprentices «— three of whom now work in other trades».

choices.text: — three of whom now work in other trades —
, three of who now work in other trades
; three of whom now work in other trades

why.A: A single dash can introduce a trailing addition at the end of a sentence. Nothing follows it, so nothing needs closing.
why.B: A closing dash promises the sentence continues, and it does not.
why.C: "Who" is the subject form; here the pronoun is the object of "of", so it has to be "whom".
why.D: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on its right, and this is a relative clause.

context: Nakata learned the words from a man «who» had learned them in the 1930s.

why.A: The pronoun is the subject of "had learned", and the subject form is "who".
why.B: "Whom" is the object form. Test it by substituting he/him: *he* had learned them, so "who".
why.C: "Which" refers to things, and the antecedent here is a man.
why.D: "Whose" is possessive and would need a noun after it.

context: Three of the four apprentices now work in other trades. «Similarly,» the fourth has stayed.

why.A: Three left and one stayed. The second sentence exists to mark the exception, and "by contrast" is the signal for an exception.
why.B: "Similarly" claims the fourth did what the other three did, which is the reverse of the fact.
why.C: "As a result" claims the fourth stayed because the others left, a causal link the passage never draws.
why.D: Three left and one stayed is a contrast, and deleting the transition asks the reader to supply it. The sentence reads as a fourth item in a list instead of an exception to one.

context: Nakata «doesn’t get all misty about» the decline of her trade.

why.A: The article’s register is measured throughout, and "not sentimental" states the point plainly.
why.B: "Gets all misty" is colloquial in a way nothing else in the piece is.
why.C: Casual in the same way, and it also softens the claim from "unsentimental" to "not very troubled".
why.D: Refusing to acknowledge a decline is a different claim — and a false one, since she describes vinyl’s advantages herself.

context: The writer wants to place the sentence "A notice about parking does not need to be beautiful." Where does it best belong?

choices.text: Immediately after "cheaper and faster is the correct answer."
As the opening sentence of the passage.
In the paragraph describing the trade’s vocabulary.
As the last sentence of the passage.

why.A: It is the concrete case for the concession just made. Placed there, it shows what "most of what a sign has to do" covers.
why.B: Opening on parking notices would put a supporting example before anything it supports.
why.C: That paragraph is about the layout, the pounce pattern and the quill, and a parking notice has nothing to do with them.
why.D: The passage ends on the trade’s survival. A concession about parking notices would undercut the close for no reason.

context: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Vinyl is cheaper and faster, she says, and for most of what a sign has to do, cheaper and faster is the correct answer." Should it be deleted?

choices.text: No, because it shows her argument is a narrow one.
No, because it gives the price difference between vinyl and painted work.
Yes, because it contradicts her decision to go on painting.
Yes, because the comparison with vinyl has already been made in the previous paragraph.

why.A: Everything after it depends on the concession. Without it the paragraph that begins "What she argues for is narrower" has nothing to be narrower than.
why.B: The price comparison is in the first paragraph. This sentence gives no figures.
why.C: It does not contradict her; it is what makes her position defensible rather than nostalgic.
why.D: The previous paragraph compares cost and speed. This sentence concedes the point, which is different work.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to show that a craft can survive by doing what its replacement cannot. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it hands the ordinary work to vinyl and locates the craft’s value on site.
Yes, because it reports how many years Nakata has worked.
No, because it concedes that vinyl is cheaper and faster than anything cut by hand in the shop.
No, because three of her four apprentices left the trade for steadier work.

why.A: The third paragraph names what a printer cannot do — space letters by eye, in the real light, at the real reading distance — and the fourth apprentice’s testimony confirms the skill transfers rather than expires.
why.B: Fifty-one years measures her career, not what the craft can do that vinyl cannot.
why.C: The concession is what makes the argument work. A claim that survives an honest concession is stronger, not weaker.
why.D: The fourth stayed, and the closing paragraph treats the trade as having outlasted several announcements of its death.

context: Ellery «disagreed to the assumption» that traffic would keep growing at four percent a year forever.

why.A: "Disagree to" is not an English construction. You agree to a proposal, but you disagree with a claim or a person.
why.B: "Disagree with" is the idiom. The preposition is fixed by usage, not by the meaning of the parts.
why.C: "Disagree from" borrows the preposition that belongs to "differ from".
why.D: "Disagree against" doubles the opposition, since disagreement is already an opposing stance.

context: By 1985 the bridge «carries» fewer cars than it had when she started counting.

why.A: The present tense clashes with "By 1985" and with "had when she started", both of which place the sentence in the past.
why.B: The past progressive matches "By 1985" and sits correctly against the past perfect "had" later in the sentence.
why.C: The future tense describes something still to come, but 1985 has already passed in the essay.
why.D: The present perfect connects a past event to now, which contradicts the fixed past date.

context: «Standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, the totals were recorded» in a hardbound ledger.

choices.text: Standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, she recorded the totals
The totals, standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, were recorded
Standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, the ledger recorded the totals

why.A: The opening phrase describes a person standing, but the subject that follows is "the totals", which cannot stand anywhere.
why.B: The subject right after the phrase is "she", and she is the one standing. The modifier now attaches to what it describes.
why.C: Moving the phrase into the middle does not change what it modifies — it still reaches for "the totals".
why.D: This gives the ledger the tally counters and the standing, which is no better than giving them to the totals.

context: The city engineers and «her» disagreed about how wide the replacement bridge should be.

why.A: "Her" is an object form, and this word is part of the compound subject doing the disagreeing.
why.B: Strip the sentence to one subject and the ear settles it: "she disagreed", not "her disagreed".
why.C: "Hers" is a possessive standing in for a noun, and nothing here is being possessed.
why.D: A reflexive needs an earlier mention of the same person in the sentence to point back to.

context: Ellery counted the cars, recorded the totals, and «was keeping» the ledgers in a consistent hand.

why.A: The first two items are simple past verbs. A past progressive in the third slot breaks the pattern the list has set.
why.B: "Counted, recorded, and kept" — three simple past verbs, all in the same form.
why.C: The past perfect progressive puts the third item further back in time than the other two, which the sentence does not intend.
why.D: "Would keep" shifts into a conditional or habitual mood the other two items are not in.

context: The eleven volumes of pencil in a consistent hand «is» now in the municipal archive.

why.A: The subject is "volumes", which is plural. "Pencil" is inside a prepositional phrase and cannot govern the verb.
why.B: "The eleven volumes ... are" — the verb matches the plural subject across the intervening phrase.
why.C: "Was" is singular as well as past, so it disagrees on both counts with a plural subject and the present-tense "now".
why.D: "Has been" is singular, and it is the nearest noun rather than the subject that makes it sound acceptable.

context: She stood at the east abutment «with a mechanical tally counter, in each hand» and recorded the totals.

choices.text: with a mechanical tally counter in each hand
with a mechanical tally counter in each hand,
with a mechanical, tally counter in each hand

why.A: The comma splits a prepositional phrase from the phrase that completes it, separating "counter" from where the counters were.
why.B: No comma belongs anywhere inside this phrase, and none belongs before "and", which joins two verbs sharing one subject.
why.C: A comma before "and recorded" would announce a second independent clause, but no new subject follows.
why.D: "Mechanical tally counter" is a single stacked description, not two coordinate adjectives, so no comma separates them.

context: The new bridge is six lanes wide, and «it has never at any time in its history carried» six lanes of traffic.

choices.text: it has not ever at any point carried
there has never been a time when it carried

why.A: "Never", "at any time" and "in its history" all say the same thing. Only one of them is doing any work.
why.B: "Has never carried" says everything the long version says, in three words.
why.C: This swaps one redundant phrase for another without removing the redundancy.
why.D: This turns a direct statement into an "there has been" construction, adding words and burying the verb.

context: In 1979 the growth «stopped, in 1981 it reversed».

why.A: Two complete sentences joined by nothing but a comma — the classic comma splice.
why.B: A semicolon is exactly what joins two closely related independent clauses with no conjunction.
why.C: This moves 1981 onto the wrong clause, saying the growth stopped in 1981, and still splices what follows.
why.D: Adding a second comma makes "in 1981" look like an interruption and leaves the two sentences still spliced.

context: For every crossing, the ledger recorded«: the date, the direction, and the count».

choices.text: the date, the direction, and the count
; the date, the direction, and the count
the date: the direction, and the count

why.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence. "The ledger recorded" is not complete — "recorded" is still waiting for its object.
why.B: The list is the direct object of "recorded", so it attaches straight to the verb with no punctuation at all.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and a three-item list is not a sentence.
why.D: This puts a colon in the middle of the list, separating the first item from the other two for no reason.

context: The new bridge «— built to the original specification,» has never carried six lanes of traffic.

why.A: A dash on one side and a comma on the other. Whichever mark is used, the same one has to close the interruption that opened it.
why.B: Correct — matched dashes hold the modifier apart from "The new bridge has never carried six lanes of traffic", which is the claim being made.
why.C: Same mismatch in the other direction — a comma cannot open what a dash closes.
why.D: With no punctuation at all, "The new bridge built to the original specification" reads as one noun phrase and the interruption disappears.

context: The plans were drawn and the money was appropriated. «Therefore,» Ellery drove out before dawn and counted the cars anyway.

why.A: "Therefore" claims the counting followed from the plans being settled, but the settled plans are the reason not to count.
why.B: The word "anyway" at the end of the sentence already signals a contrast, and "Still" is the transition that matches it.
why.C: "Likewise" claims the second sentence is a parallel case, and counting cars is not parallel to appropriating money.
why.D: "In addition" adds an item to a list, but this sentence works against the previous one rather than extending it.

context: Ellery is «careless» about how she tells this story, and she does not claim she was right and the engineers were wrong.

why.A: "Careless" means the opposite of what the rest of the sentence shows: someone declining to overclaim is being precise, not sloppy.
why.B: "Careful" matches the restraint the sentence goes on to describe.
why.C: "Carefree" means untroubled, which says nothing about how precisely she tells it.
why.D: "Caring" describes warmth toward people, not precision about a claim.

context: The writer is considering deleting the clause "and the plans were drawn, and the money was appropriated" from the first paragraph. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it establishes that the decision was already settled when the counting began.
Kept, because it tells the reader what year the original bridge was built.
Deleted, because the essay is about traffic counts rather than about how construction was financed.
Deleted, because it repeats information the paragraph has already given.

why.A: The essay turns on the counting having no official purpose. Without the settled plans and the appropriated money, there is nothing for the counting to be pointless against.
why.B: The paragraph gives 1974 as the replacement date, not the construction date, and the deleted clause does not supply either.
why.C: The financing is what shows the decision was closed, so it is doing work for the essay rather than wandering from it.
why.D: Nothing earlier in the paragraph mentions the plans or the money, so the clause is not a repetition.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to show why a forecast has to be checked against what actually happened. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it sets a four-percent growth model against an eleven-year record showing the opposite.
Yes, because it describes the mechanical tally counters that Ellery held in each hand at the roadside.
No, because the essay concerns a single bridge and never once uses the word forecast.
No, because Ellery herself signed the report that recommended the replacement.

why.A: This names the two things the essay puts in opposition — a projection and a record — and the point Ellery draws from the gap between them.
why.B: The counters are a detail of method. They show how she counted, not why checking a projection matters.
why.C: One extended case is a normal way to make a general point, and the essay states the general point outright in its final lines.
why.D: Her agreement with the replacement is what keeps her narrower claim credible; it does not undercut the essay’s purpose.

context: The eleven dishes she cooked for fifty years «was» never written down.

why.A: "Was" is singular, and the subject is "the eleven dishes".
why.B: "The eleven dishes ... were" — a plural subject takes a plural verb, whatever comes between them.
why.C: "Has been" is also singular, and the relative clause between subject and verb does not change what the verb must agree with.
why.D: "Is" is singular and present, so it disagrees in number and clashes with the past-tense "cooked".

context: My grandmother and «me» spent four weekends in her kitchen with a scale and a notebook.

why.A: "Me" is an object form, and this word is half of the compound subject that does the spending.
why.B: Drop the other half and the choice is obvious: "I spent four weekends", not "me spent four weekends".
why.C: "Myself" is reflexive and needs an earlier "I" in the sentence to refer back to.
why.D: "Mine" is possessive and replaces a noun, which is not what this slot needs.

context: By the time I turned twenty-six, she «makes» the same eleven dishes for half a century.

why.A: The present tense cannot describe something that had already run for fifty years before a past moment.
why.B: The past perfect progressive is built for exactly this: an action running up to a point in the past.
why.C: The present progressive places the cooking now, not before the writer turned twenty-six.
why.D: The future perfect looks forward from the present, and "By the time I turned" looks back.

context: «Weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, the measurements were astonishingly consistent.»

choices.text: Weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, I found the measurements astonishingly consistent.
The measurements, weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, were astonishingly consistent.
Weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, the consistency was astonishing.

why.A: The opening phrase needs someone doing the weighing, and the subject that arrives is "the measurements", which did no weighing.
why.B: "I" follows the phrase and "I" did the weighing, so the modifier finally has something to attach to.
why.C: Relocating the phrase changes nothing — it still modifies "the measurements".
why.D: This hands the weighing to "the consistency", which is an abstraction and cannot hold a scale.

context: Garlic burns at a lower temperature than onion does, so it is «susceptible of» turning bitter.

why.A: "Susceptible of" survives in legal and technical writing meaning "admits of", but it is not the idiom for being vulnerable to something.
why.B: "Susceptible to" is the standard idiom for being liable to suffer something.
why.C: "Susceptible for" is not an English pairing.
why.D: "Susceptible with" is not an English pairing either.

context: She learned the sequence by standing beside her mother, by watching her hands, and «she repeated it» for six decades.

why.A: The first two items are "by" plus a gerund. A full clause in the third slot leaves the list half-built.
why.B: "By standing, by watching, and by repeating" — all three items now take the same shape.
why.C: Dropping "by" leaves a bare past-tense verb, which does not match two prepositional phrases.
why.D: "Having repeated" is a perfect participle, which marks the repeating as finished before the learning rather than part of it.

context: I have the eleven recipes now, written in «my grandmothers hand» and annotated in mine.

why.A: The hand belongs to the grandmother, and possession needs an apostrophe.
why.B: One grandmother, so the apostrophe goes before the s.
why.C: An apostrophe after the s marks a plural possessive, but the essay describes one grandmother.
why.D: This stacks two apostrophes, which no possessive form in English uses.

context: My grandmother«, who was eighty-three that year» had decided long ago that nothing needed writing down.

why.A: The clause is set off at the front but never closed, so the comma opens an interruption the sentence does not finish.
why.B: A nonessential clause takes a comma at both ends — remove what sits between them and the sentence still stands.
why.C: Closing without opening is the same error in the other direction.
why.D: With no commas the clause reads as essential, implying the writer has other grandmothers and means the eighty-three-year-old one.

context: She was not improvising. «Executing a recipe she had run several thousand times.»

choices.text: She was executing a recipe she had run several thousand times.
Executing a recipe, she had run several thousand times.
A recipe she had run several thousand times, executing it.

why.A: "Executing" is a participle, not a verb with a subject, so this group of words has no main clause.
why.B: Adding the subject and the helping verb turns the participle into a predicate and the fragment into a sentence.
why.C: The comma makes "she had run several thousand times" the main clause and leaves the recipe with no object to attach to.
why.D: This reorders the fragment without ever supplying a subject and a main verb.

context: What she could not do was «to give an explanation of the reason why» the onions went in before the garlic.

choices.text: give an explanation as to the reason
explain the reason as to why

why.A: "Give an explanation of the reason why" takes seven words to say what "explain why" says in two.
why.B: "Explain why" carries the whole meaning, and the verb does the work the noun phrase was doing.
why.C: This trades one padded phrase for another and drops the "why" the sentence still needs.
why.D: "The reason as to why" stacks three ways of saying the same thing.

context: Her cupped hand was more consistent than most people manage with a measuring cup. «For example,» she could not say how much it held.

why.A: Not being able to state the amount is not an example of being consistent; it works against it.
why.B: "Even so" concedes the first sentence and then sets the limitation against it, which is the relation here.
why.C: "Therefore" claims the inability follows from the consistency, and it does not.
why.D: The essay turns on the gap between doing a thing well and being able to say how, so the concession has to be marked. Deleted, the two sentences read as unrelated observations.

context: I am not sure this is an improvement so much as a translation; the notebook has «affected» a change in where the knowledge lives.

why.A: "Affect" as a verb means to influence something that already exists. The sentence needs the sense of bringing the change about.
why.B: "Effect" used as a verb means to bring about, which is exactly what a change requires here.
why.C: The bare form does not fit after "has", which needs a past participle.
why.D: "Effect" as a noun cannot follow "has" in this construction either.

context: The measurements were astonishingly consistent «— ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four,» which is a tighter tolerance than most cooks manage.

choices.text: — ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four —
, ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four —
ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four

why.A: The three weights are introduced by a dash and dismissed by a comma, so nothing marks the point where the figures end and the comment on them begins.
why.B: Correct — the figures are bracketed by dashes, which is what lets the "which" clause attach to the consistency rather than to ninety-four grams.
why.C: Same mismatch reversed, and a comma cannot open an interruption that already contains commas without confusing the reader.
why.D: With no punctuation the three readings run straight into the sentence and the reader cannot tell where the interruption ends.

context: The writer is considering adding the sentence "Garlic burns at a lower temperature than onion and turns bitter." Should it be added?

choices.text: Yes, because it supplies the reason the grandmother followed without being able to state it.
Yes, because it explains why the writer decided to buy a kitchen scale.
No, because the essay never otherwise mentions garlic.
No, because it contradicts the claim that the grandmother got the sequence right every single time.

why.A: The whole essay turns on a rule that worked without a stated reason. The sentence is that missing reason, and the gap it fills is the essay’s subject.
why.B: The scale was bought to record quantities, and nothing about garlic chemistry bears on that decision.
why.C: The garlic and onion sequence is exactly what the writer asks about and cannot get an answer to.
why.D: It explains why her sequence was right. Supplying the reason for a correct rule does not contradict its correctness.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to examine the difference between knowing how to do something and being able to explain it. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows a cook running a sequence reliably for sixty years without being able to say why it worked.
Yes, because it lists all eleven of the dishes the grandmother made without ever writing down a recipe for any of them.
No, because the essay is about recipes rather than about knowledge of any kind.
No, because the writer eventually located the reason in a textbook.

why.A: This names both halves of the distinction and the single person who displays the gap between them.
why.B: The essay never lists the dishes, and a list would show what she cooked rather than what she knew.
why.C: The recipes are the occasion. What the essay actually examines is what was and was not transmitted along with them.
why.D: Finding the reason afterward is what makes the gap visible — it shows the rule was right and the explanation was simply missing.

context: A watershed that once released its rainfall over several days now «release» it in a few hours.

why.A: The subject is the singular "a watershed". The relative clause between it and the verb does not change what the verb agrees with.
why.B: "A watershed ... releases" — singular subject, singular verb.
why.C: "Have released" is plural and shifts to the present perfect, neither of which the sentence supports.
why.D: "Are releasing" is plural as well, and the nearest noun, "days", is not the subject.

context: For most of the twentieth century, the guiding principle of urban drainage «is» speed.

why.A: The present tense contradicts "For most of the twentieth century", which closes the period off in the past.
why.B: A completed stretch of past time takes the simple past.
why.C: The present perfect would mean the principle still governs, which is what the rest of the passage argues has changed.
why.D: The future tense places the principle ahead of us rather than behind us.

context: Cities had not eliminated «they’re» flooding; they had exported it downstream.

why.A: "They’re" is a contraction of "they are", which gives "had not eliminated they are flooding".
why.B: "Their" is the possessive form, and the flooding belongs to the cities.
why.C: "There" points at a place and cannot show possession.
why.D: "Theirs" stands alone in place of a noun and cannot sit in front of one.

context: The older designs paved the channel, straightened the creek, and «the water was buried» in a culvert.

why.A: The first two items are active past-tense verbs with the designs as subject. The third switches to a passive clause with a different subject.
why.B: "Paved, straightened, and buried" — three active past-tense verbs sharing one subject.
why.C: A gerund does not match two finite verbs.
why.D: A noun phrase cannot sit in a list whose other members are verbs.

context: «Ignored for three years, a city discovers that a rain garden becomes a weed patch that does not drain.»

choices.text: A rain garden ignored for three years becomes a weed patch that does not drain.
Ignored for three years, the discovery is that a rain garden becomes a weed patch that does not drain.
A city, ignored for three years, discovers that a rain garden becomes a weed patch that does not drain.

why.A: The opening phrase lands on "a city", so the sentence says the city was ignored for three years rather than the garden.
why.B: The phrase now sits directly against "a rain garden", which is the thing actually being ignored.
why.C: This attaches the neglect to "the discovery", which is no more capable of being ignored for three years than the city was.
why.D: Moving the phrase into commas after "a city" states outright what the original merely implied — that the city was ignored.

context: The newer designs are «different than» the older ones in one respect above all.

why.A: "Different than" is common in speech but is not the form tested as standard, and "than" belongs with comparatives such as "larger" or "slower".
why.B: "Different from" is the standard idiom, and the two things compared sit on either side of it.
why.C: "Different to" is British usage rather than the American standard the test follows.
why.D: "Than that of" adds a comparison to a possessed thing, which leaves "the older ones" with nothing to belong to.

context: A rain garden is a shallow depression planted with deep-rooted species «, that takes runoff from a roof and lets it soak in.»

choices.text: that takes runoff from a roof and lets it soak in.
which takes runoff from a roof, and lets it soak in.
, that takes runoff from a roof, and lets it soak in.

why.A: A clause beginning with "that" is essential to the noun it modifies, and an essential clause never takes a comma before it.
why.B: No comma before "that", and none before "and", which joins two verbs sharing the same subject.

context: The 1986 instrument sounded better than anything he has made since. «Similarly,» it was unplayable within eight years.

why.A: "Similarly" presents the second fact as another of the same kind, and one is a success while the other is a failure.
why.B: The two facts are both true of the same instrument and pull in opposite directions, which is what "also, however" marks.
why.C: "As a result" claims the failure followed from the sound, and the passage locates the cause in the soundboard’s thinness instead.
why.D: "In other words" restates, and the second sentence says something new.

context: Within the third paragraph, the sentence "It sounded, by his own account, better than anything he had made before or has made since" belongs where it is because it:

choices.text: introduces the 1986 instrument to the reader for the first time.
explains why Huang bought the instrument back.
summarises the paragraph’s argument before any of the evidence for it has been given.

why.A: A failure is only instructive if the thing that failed was worth having. Placing the praise first is what makes the eight-year collapse a trade rather than a mistake.
why.B: The previous sentence already introduces it as the instrument he considers his worst.
why.C: The buyback is explained by the two rebuilds that precede it, not by the sound.
why.D: The paragraph has no thesis to summarise; it is narrating a case.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to show why a principle can be widely agreed on and still rarely followed. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because everyone accepts it and nobody applies it.
Yes, because it explains in detail how a harpsichord responds to changes in the humidity of the room it is standing in.
No, because Huang says he would not do anything differently now.
No, because the passage concerns a single builder rather than the trade as a whole.

why.A: That sentence names both halves of the question directly — universal agreement and near-universal exception — and the 1986 instrument is the case that shows it.
why.B: The humidity explains why the problem exists, not why the principle goes unfollowed.
why.C: He says the opposite: he would make the soundboard thicker and accept a smaller sound.
why.D: One builder is how the passage makes its point, and Huang states the principle in general terms.

context: Pell had no training as a scientist«, but she» simply continued the work when her husband died.

why.A: Correct — two independent clauses joined by a comma and a coordinating conjunction, which is one of the four ways English lets you join them.
why.B: A comma alone cannot hold two independent clauses together. Without "but" this is a splice.
why.C: The conjunction is there but the comma is not, and a compound sentence of this length needs both.
why.D: A sentence may open with "But", but not with a comma after it; nothing is being set off.

context: The entries in the ledger «were» spare: wind direction, cloud cover, and the hour the lamp was lit.

why.A: Correct — the subject is "entries", and the phrase "in the ledger" that follows it does not change what the verb has to agree with.
why.B: Agrees with "ledger" rather than with "entries". The prepositional phrase is not the subject.
why.C: Singular and in the wrong tense; everything around it describes a record kept in the past.
why.D: Singular, and the present perfect suggests the entries are still being written.

context: «Because she had no reason to think anyone would read the notes, she kept them for herself.»

choices.text: Because she had no reason to think anyone would read the notes.
Having no reason to think anyone would read the notes.
Because she had no reason to think anyone would read the notes, keeping them for herself.

why.A: Correct — a subordinate clause followed by a main clause that gives it a subject and a verb of its own.
why.B: A subordinate clause with nothing to attach to. "Because" always promises a main clause that never arrives here.
why.C: A participial phrase, which cannot stand as a sentence no matter how much information it carries.
why.D: The main clause has been turned into a participle, so nothing in the sentence is a finite verb.

context: «Pell’s» ledger reached back into the 1880s, and it was continuous.

why.A: Correct — one keeper, so the possessive is the name plus apostrophe-s.
why.B: A plural with no apostrophe, which says there were several Pells and claims nothing for any of them.
why.C: The plural possessive. There is only one Pell in the passage.
why.D: Pluralises the name and then makes the plural possessive, compounding both errors.

context: «Looking for shipping records, Alcantara opened the almanac instead.»

choices.text: Looking for shipping records, the almanac was opened instead.
The almanac, looking for shipping records, was opened by Alcantara instead.
Looking for shipping records, it was the almanac that was opened instead.

why.A: Correct — the person doing the looking is the subject of the main clause, which is what an opening participial phrase requires.
why.B: The almanac was not looking for shipping records. The participle has nothing to modify but the subject it is given.
why.C: Puts the phrase beside "almanac", which makes the ledger the one conducting the search.
why.D: The subject is now "it", so the search belongs to nothing in the sentence at all.

context: Read together, those columns recorded «when the ice broke, when the ducks arrived, and when the herring ran.»

choices.text: when the ice broke, the arrival of the ducks, and when the herring ran.
the ice breaking, when the ducks arrived, and the herring running.
when the ice broke, the ducks arriving, and the running of the herring.

why.A: Correct — three clauses of the same shape, each opening with "when" and each with its own subject and past-tense verb.
why.B: The middle item becomes a noun phrase while the two around it stay clauses.
why.C: Two gerund phrases with a clause wedged between them; no two items match.
why.D: Three different constructions in three slots: a clause, a participial phrase, and a noun phrase.

context: Alcantara «spent two years transcribing» the almanac.

choices.text: spent a period of two years in the transcription of
used up two years of time transcribing
spent two years engaged in the transcribing of

why.A: Correct — the verb takes the gerund directly, and nothing in the sentence is doing work twice.
why.B: "A period of" says only what "two years" already says, and the noun form of transcribe adds a preposition for nothing.
why.C: Two years is already a quantity of time, so "of time" is empty.
why.D: "Engaged in the transcribing of" is four words where "transcribing" was enough.

context: In 1994 a graduate student «named Teodoro Alcantara» opened it instead.

why.A: Correct — "a graduate student" has not identified anyone yet, so the name is doing necessary work and takes no commas.
why.B: Commas would make the name an aside, as though the reader already knew which student was meant.
why.C: A comma after "named" separates the participle from the name it introduces.
why.D: One comma opens an interruption that is never closed.

context: Researchers had plenty of instrument data from the twentieth century and almost none from before it. Pell’s ledger, «by contrast,» reached back into the 1880s.

why.A: Correct — the ledger is set against the gap just described, and that opposition is what the sentence turns on.
why.B: The ledger is not an instance of the shortage; it is the exception to it.
why.C: Adding would suggest the ledger is more of the same scarce data rather than the thing that fills the gap.
why.D: The ledger did not come about because the record was thin. It was kept decades before anyone noticed the gap.

context: That trend «has since been corroborated» by three other regional records.

why.A: Correct — the present perfect covers a stretch reaching from the discovery up to now, which is what "since" asks for.
why.B: The past perfect puts the corroboration before some earlier past event, and no such event is named.
why.C: The future contradicts "since", which looks back from the present.
why.D: The progressive makes corroborating an activity still underway; the three records already exist.

context: The inspectors who visited every spring found the brass polished and the ledger current, and «they» never noticed the extra columns.

why.A: Correct — the antecedent is "inspectors", which is plural and human, so the plural pronoun is the only one that fits.
why.B: Singular and non-human. The nearest plausible antecedent is a group of people.
why.C: Singular, and the passage never narrows the inspectors down to one man.
why.D: "One" generalises to anybody at all, which loses the inspectors the sentence is about.

context: Pell had no training as a scientist«; nevertheless, she» kept the most complete coastal record of her century.

why.A: Correct — a semicolon joins the two statements and the conjunctive adverb, set off by its comma, names the relation between them.
why.B: "Nevertheless" is not a conjunction, so a comma on each side of it leaves two independent clauses spliced together.
why.C: No punctuation at all between two complete statements, which fuses them.
why.D: The semicolon has already done the joining; adding "and" joins it twice.

context: The inspectors «visited» every spring.

choices.text: came for the purpose of a visit
paid a visit on a yearly basis

why.A: Correct — one verb carries the whole action, and "every spring" already says how often.
why.B: Turns a verb into a noun and then needs a second verb to carry it.
why.C: "For the purpose of" announces an intention the sentence never needed.
why.D: "On a yearly basis" repeats what "every spring" has already established.

context: The city had no interest in the number«;» the bridge was scheduled for replacement in 1974.

why.A: Correct — two statements that could each stand alone, closely enough related that a semicolon is better than a full stop.
why.B: A comma between two independent clauses is a splice, whatever the relation between them.
why.C: With nothing between them the two statements fuse into one ungrammatical sentence.
why.D: "Because" turns the second half into a subordinate clause, which cannot follow a semicolon.

context: The plans for the replacement «were» drawn, and the money was appropriated.

why.A: Correct — "plans" is the subject, and "for the replacement" sits between it and the verb without changing the agreement.
why.B: Agrees with "replacement", the nearest noun, rather than with the subject.
why.C: Singular, and the present perfect sits oddly beside "was appropriated" in the second half.
why.D: Singular and present, in a sentence about what happened before 1974.

context: «Standing at the east abutment, Ellery held a mechanical tally counter in each hand.»

choices.text: Standing at the east abutment, a mechanical tally counter was held in each hand.
A mechanical tally counter was in each hand, standing at the east abutment.
Held in each hand, Ellery stood at the east abutment with a mechanical tally counter.

why.A: Correct — Ellery is both the one standing and the subject of the main clause, which is what the opening participle needs.
why.B: The counters are not standing anywhere; the passive has removed the only thing that could be.
why.C: Same dangling participle, now at the end of the sentence, where it attaches to the counter.
why.D: "Held in each hand" lands on Ellery, which says she was the thing being held.

context: Ellery «counted» the cars that crossed the bridge.

why.A: Correct — the verb does the work on its own and takes its object directly.
why.B: Buries the verb in a noun and needs "made" plus "of" to get it back.
why.C: Three words of scaffolding around a verb that needed none.
why.D: "Performed a count upon" is both padded and wrong about the preposition.

context: She stood at the abutment, «recorded the totals in a ledger, and drove home before the traffic thickened.»

choices.text: recorded the totals in a ledger, and was driving home before the traffic thickened.
recording the totals in a ledger, and drove home before the traffic thickened.
recorded the totals in a ledger, and her drive home came before the traffic thickened.

why.A: Correct — three simple past verbs hanging off one subject: stood, recorded, drove.
why.B: The third verb shifts into the past progressive while the first two stay simple.
why.C: A participle in the second slot breaks the series the first and third keep.
why.D: The third item becomes a clause with a new subject, so the sentence stops being a list of what she did.

context: «Ellery’s» ledgers are in the municipal archive now.

why.A: Correct — one engineer, so the name takes an apostrophe and an s to claim the ledgers.
why.B: No apostrophe, so nothing is possessed; this reads as a plural of the surname.
why.C: Invents a plural of the name and then makes it possessive.
why.D: An apostrophe on each end, which no possessive form uses.

context: «The model was never checked against anything, and hers was the only number in the room that had been.»

choices.text: The model never checked against anything, and hers the only number in the room that had been.
Because the model was never checked against anything, and hers was the only number in the room that had been.
The model was never checked against anything. Hers being the only number in the room that had been.

why.A: Correct — two independent clauses, each with a subject and a finite verb, joined by a comma and "and".
why.B: Both halves lose their verbs: "never checked" needs "was", and "hers the only number" has no verb at all.
why.C: "Because" subordinates everything that follows, leaving the whole sentence without a main clause.
why.D: The second sentence is a participial phrase, which cannot stand on its own however long it is.

context: By 1985 the bridge was carrying fewer cars than it had when she started. The four-percent model, «however,» had projected a figure roughly double the one her ledger showed.

why.A: Correct — the model and the ledger point in opposite directions, and that disagreement is the whole point of the paragraph.
why.B: The projection did not follow from the decline; it preceded it and got it wrong.
why.C: The model is not an example of falling traffic. It predicted the opposite.
why.D: "Likewise" claims the two agree, which is exactly what the sentence is denying.

context: Ellery«, who is ninety-one,» is careful about how she tells this.

why.A: Correct — her age does not pick her out from other Elleries, so the clause is an aside and takes a comma at each end.
why.B: Without commas the clause reads as restrictive, as though it were distinguishing this Ellery from another one.
why.C: Opens the interruption and never closes it, so the reader cannot tell where the main clause resumes.
why.D: Closes an interruption that was never opened.

context: A graduate student «found» them in 2019 and built a paper around them.

why.A: Correct — a single completed event with its year attached, which the simple past is for, and it matches "built" beside it.
why.B: The present tense fights the date. 2019 is over.
why.C: The present perfect cannot take a stated past time like "in 2019".
why.D: The past perfect would need a later past event for the finding to precede.

context: The paper’s central point is one «she» had made in a letter forty years earlier.

why.A: Correct — the pronoun is the subject of "had made" inside the relative clause, so it takes the subject form.
why.B: The object form, which cannot be the thing doing the making.
why.C: A reflexive needs a subject elsewhere in the clause to refer back to, and there is none.
why.D: A possessive standing where the sentence needs a subject.

context: Ellery had signed the inspection report that recommended the replacement«. She agreed» with it.

why.A: Correct — two complete statements, and the full stop between them lets the short second one land.
why.B: A comma cannot join two independent clauses on its own.
why.C: Nothing between them at all, so the two statements run together.
why.D: The comma after "and" separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

context: What she claims is «narrower and harder to argue with.»

choices.text: of a narrower nature and harder to argue with.
more narrow in scope and more difficult in terms of arguing with.
narrower, and it is harder to argue with it.

why.A: Correct — two comparative adjectives sharing one verb, with nothing between them that does not carry meaning.
why.B: "Of a narrower nature" is four words for the comparative the adjective already has.
why.C: "In scope" and "in terms of" are both filler, and "more narrow" ignores the shorter comparative form.
why.D: Splits one comparison into two clauses and repeats the pronoun to do it.

context: I walked the aisles with a handheld logger«, and I confirmed» that the temperature at each station matched what the central system claimed.

why.A: Correct — a comma plus "and" joining two independent clauses, each with its own subject and verb.
why.B: Removing the conjunction leaves a comma holding two full clauses together, which it cannot do.
why.C: The conjunction without the comma runs a compound sentence of this length together.
why.D: A semicolon already joins the clauses, so "and" is redundant, and the comma after it is wrong.

context: The temperature at each of forty stations «matched» what the central system claimed it was.

why.A: Correct — the subject is the singular "temperature", and "at each of forty stations" is a prepositional phrase, not a plural subject.
why.B: Plural, agreeing with "stations" instead of with "temperature".
why.C: Plural and progressive, both wrong for a single nightly check that either matched or did not.
why.D: Plural, and the present perfect reads as though the checking were still going on.

context: A system that reports on itself «will report» that it is fine right up until it cannot.

choices.text: will make a report to the effect

why.A: Correct — the verb the sentence has already used once, used again in the same plain form for the same action.
why.B: "Make a report to the effect" is five words doing what "report" does in one.
why.C: The progressive future makes the reporting an ongoing activity when what is meant is what the system will do.
why.D: Pairs a vague verb with the noun form of the real one.

context: «Standing in the airlock in a borrowed parka, I learned that the twenty minutes was not a suggestion.»

choices.text: Standing in the airlock in a borrowed parka, the twenty minutes turned out not to be a suggestion.
The twenty minutes, standing in the airlock in a borrowed parka, was not a suggestion.
In a borrowed parka standing in the airlock, it was learned that the twenty minutes was not a suggestion.

why.A: Correct — the narrator is the one standing in the airlock and the subject of the main clause, so the phrase has something to modify.
why.B: Twenty minutes cannot stand in an airlock wearing a parka.
why.C: The phrase now sits inside the subject, which makes the time limit the one in the parka.
why.D: The passive removes the person entirely, leaving the phrase attached to "it".

context: «Both were a tenth of a degree, and both were explained by a sensor that needed recalibrating.»

choices.text: Both of them a tenth of a degree, and both of them explained by a sensor that needed recalibrating.
Both a tenth of a degree, both explained by a sensor that needed recalibrating.
Being a tenth of a degree each, and explained by a sensor that needed recalibrating.

why.A: Correct — two clauses, each with a subject and a finite verb, joined by a comma and "and".
why.B: Neither half has a verb; "explained" is a participle here, not a predicate.
why.C: Two phrases in apposition with nothing to be in apposition to.
why.D: Opens with a participle and never reaches a subject or a main verb.

context: What I was doing in the cold was not measuring the temperature«; it was making sure there were two independent answers to the question.»

choices.text: ; it was to make sure there were two independent answers to the question.
; but to make sure there were two independent answers to the question.
; making sure there were two independent answers to the question.

why.A: Correct — "was making" answers "was not measuring" in the same form, which is what the contrast needs to land.
why.B: An infinitive on one side of the contrast and a gerund on the other.
why.C: "But" after a semicolon, and an infinitive set against a gerund.
why.D: A participial phrase with no subject or verb, which cannot follow a semicolon.

context: A system that reports on itself will report that «it’s» fine right up until it cannot.

why.A: Correct — the sentence needs "it is", and the apostrophe marks the missing letter of the contraction.
why.B: The possessive, which would have the system owning a "fine" rather than being in one.
why.C: No such form exists. "Its" is already possessive and never takes an apostrophe.
why.D: "It has fine" is not a sentence; the contraction here stands for "it is".

context: For the first few months this struck me as an elaborate way of proving that a thermometer works. «Then» a storage manager from another seed bank came through on a tour.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph is narrating a change of mind, and the visit is what came next in that sequence.
why.B: The visit is not another instance of the job feeling pointless; it is what stopped it feeling that way.
why.C: A visiting manager is not an example of an elaborate proof.
why.D: A contrast marker would set the visit against the first few months, but the sentence is simply what happened after them.

context: The job posting said "facility technician"« and» did not mention that the facility was kept at minus eighteen degrees.

why.A: Correct — one subject with two verbs, "said" and "did not mention", and a compound predicate takes no comma before the conjunction.
why.B: The comma suggests a second independent clause, but what follows has no subject of its own.
why.C: Supplying "it" creates a second clause, which changes the sentence rather than punctuating it.
why.D: A semicolon needs a complete statement on each side, and the second half has no subject.

context: Nobody expected a mismatch, and in eleven months I «found» two.

why.A: Correct — the eleven months are over and the narrator has left the job, so the simple past closes the account, matching "expected".
why.B: The present perfect keeps the period open, but the narrator says elsewhere that the year ended.
why.C: The past perfect needs a later past moment to sit before, and none is given.
why.D: The present tense contradicts both "expected" and the eleven months already elapsed.

context: Walter Ostrowski, who is ninety-one and does not drive, had built his day «around» walking out to the box at one o’clock.

why.A: Correct — "build a day around something" is the fixed idiom for arranging a schedule to suit it.
why.B: "Round" describes encircling something physically and does not carry the sense of organising a day.
why.C: "Build a day about" is not English; "about" would mean concerning, which is not the sense here.
why.D: "Build on" means to use something as a foundation for something further, which reverses the relationship.

context: Her successor said he had not known there was anything «for knowing» about the Ostrowski box.

why.A: "Anything for knowing" is not an English construction; nothing in the sentence licenses "for" here.
why.B: Correct — "anything" takes an infinitive when what follows names what could be done: anything to know.
why.C: "Of knowing" would need a noun for the gerund to modify, and "anything" is not doing that work.
why.D: The passive clause makes the sentence say the fact is known, when the point is that it was not.

context: Within the fourth paragraph, the sentence "A route is a route" belongs where it is because it:

choices.text: restates the district's position in the plainest terms before the objection to it arrives.
introduces the 2009 call that the rest of the paragraph goes on to describe in detail.
explains why the district installed the routing software at the start of that winter.
concedes that Reyes was wrong to stop driving the order the software had produced.

why.A: Correct — it compresses the policy the writer has just granted, so the "But" that follows has something to push against.
why.B: The call is introduced by the sentence after it, not by this one, which mentions nothing about 2009.
why.C: The paragraph never takes up the district's reasons for installing the software; that is the second paragraph.
why.D: Nothing in the sentence concerns whether Reyes was right, and the paragraph goes on to argue that she noticed something real.

context: The writer is considering moving the sentence about the 2009 call to the end of the final paragraph. This move would:

choices.text: weaken the passage, because the call is the evidence that answers the district in that paragraph.
strengthen the passage, because the final paragraph is where the writer states the point directly.
weaken the passage, because the call happened years before the software was installed.
strengthen the passage, because it would leave the two dates in chronological order.

why.A: Correct — the fourth paragraph grants the policy and then answers it, and the call is the whole of the answer.
why.B: The final paragraph states the point, which is exactly why it does not also need to carry the evidence.
why.C: The call is older than the software, but that is what gives it force: the noticing predates any route plan.
why.D: Chronological order is not what the paragraph is organised by, and moving the call would break an argument to fix nothing.

context: The writer is considering deleting the detail that the new order ran 4.2 miles shorter and saved eleven minutes a day. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it grants the software a real advantage, which makes the objection worth hearing.
Kept, because it proves the district was right to reorder the route the way the software did.
Deleted, because the passage is about an elderly man rather than about mileage and minutes.
Deleted, because the figures contradict the claim that nothing was taken away from the route.

why.A: Correct — an objection to a change that had no advantage would cost the writer nothing to make.
why.B: The passage argues the opposite; conceding a saving is not the same as endorsing the decision.
why.C: Ostrowski is an example within the argument, not its subject, and the saving is what he is weighed against.
why.D: There is no contradiction: the writer says the eleven minutes were added to the route and something else went with them.

context: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the second paragraph: "Software of this kind is now used by most rural districts in the state." Should it be added?

choices.text: No, because the paragraph establishes what this route lost, which a state figure does not touch.
No, because the passage never identifies the company that wrote the routing software.
Yes, because it shows that Reyes was not the only carrier whose route was reordered.
Yes, because it establishes that the district was following ordinary practice for the state.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph is narrowing to one route and three weeks, and a figure about the state widens it back out.
why.B: Who wrote the software is not information the paragraph needs, so its absence is not a reason to add anything.
why.C: It would show that, but the paragraph is not making a claim about how many carriers were affected.
why.D: The paragraph already grants that the software was reasonable; ordinary practice adds nothing to that concession.

context: Reyes had been the one to notice that the box had not been emptied in nine days, and «it was her who» called it in.

why.A: After a form of "be" the pronoun is a predicate nominative, so the subject form is required, not "her".
why.B: Correct — "she" follows "was" as a predicate nominative, and "who" then introduces the clause about her.
why.C: This keeps the object form and swaps the relative pronoun, so the one real error is left in place.
why.D: A participial phrase leaves the clause with no verb of its own and cannot join what comes before it.

context: The district’s position was that this is not a carrier’s concern, and as a matter of policy «they were» right.

why.A: A district is one organisation, so a plural pronoun leaves the sentence without a plural antecedent.
why.B: Correct — the antecedent is "the district", a singular noun, which takes the singular "it was".
why.C: This corrects nothing about number and adds a past perfect the sentence has no earlier event to need.
why.D: "Those" is a plural demonstrative and points at nothing in the sentence that could be plural.

context: The software was not wrong about distance. «Therefore,» Reyes drove the new order for three weeks and then stopped.

why.A: "Therefore" claims that stopping follows from the software being right, which is the reverse of the sense.
why.B: Correct — she stopped despite the saving the previous sentence grants, and "even so" marks a concession.
why.C: "In addition" would add another point in the same direction, but the second sentence turns against the first.
why.D: "For instance" promises an example of the software being right about distance, and no example follows.

context: Reyes drove the new order for three «weeks and then stopped, and her» reasons are worth setting down.

choices.text: weeks, and then stopped and her
weeks and then stopped and her
weeks, and then stopped, and her

why.A: Correct — one comma before the "and" that joins two independent clauses, and none inside the compound verb.
why.B: This puts the comma inside the compound verb, separating "drove" from "then stopped", and drops it where two clauses join.
why.C: With no comma at all the two independent clauses run together at the joining "and".
why.D: The first comma still splits a compound verb, so the sentence is over-punctuated even though the second comma is right.

context: The software plans the route by the minute, reorders the ninety-eight boxes, and «it saves eleven minutes a day».

choices.text: eleven minutes a day are saved

why.A: The third item restates the subject, so the series stops being a series of verbs and becomes a clause tacked on.
why.B: Correct — "plans", "reorders" and "saves" are three verbs sharing one subject, which is what the series needs.
why.C: A participle cannot stand as the third member beside two finite verbs without breaking the pattern.
why.D: Switching to the passive changes the subject mid-series and leaves the software out of its own third action.

context: «Reordered by the software, Reyes found» the Ostrowski mailbox at 10:40 instead of 1:15.

choices.text: Because the route had been reordered, Reyes reached
Having been reordered by the software, Reyes found

why.A: The opening phrase describes whatever follows the comma, and what was reordered was the route, not Reyes.
why.B: Correct — turning the phrase into a clause gives "reordered" its own subject, so nothing is left dangling.
why.C: This makes Reyes the one doing the reordering, and it was the software that reordered the route.
why.D: The participle still has to attach to "Reyes", so lengthening it leaves the same misplacement in place.

context: For two weeks his mail «sat in the box overnight and remained there through the night until morning».

choices.text: sat overnight in the box through the night

why.A: "Overnight", "through the night" and "until morning" all say the same thing three times over.
why.B: Correct — "overnight" already carries the whole duration, so one statement of it is enough.
why.C: This cuts one repetition and keeps the other, so the sentence still says the night twice.
why.D: Cutting to "sat" loses where the mail sat, which is the detail the sentence exists to report.

context: In the third week he stopped coming out at «all, Reyes found» four days of it.

context: One tape from 1968 «— cut during a thunderstorm —» is still the clearest in the basement.

why.A: Correct — a pair of dashes fences off the aside with the same mark at each end.
why.B: An interrupter cannot open with a dash and close with a comma; the marks must match.
why.C: This mixes the two marks in the other order, which fails for the same reason.
why.D: Semicolons separate independent clauses and cannot fence off a phrase like this one.

context: Neither of the two surveys published «their» recordings in full.

why.A: "Neither" is singular, so a plural pronoun does not agree with it.
why.B: Correct — "neither" takes a singular pronoun, and the possessive form is "its".
why.C: This is the contraction of "it is", which cannot show possession of anything.
why.D: Adding "own" leaves the pronoun plural and the disagreement entirely untouched.

context: The archive of field tapes, along with the notebooks kept beside the machines, «are» stored in a basement.

why.A: The subject is "archive", and the phrase fenced off by commas cannot change its number.
why.B: Correct — "archive" is singular, so the verb that follows it is "is".
why.C: This is plural as well as past, so it disagrees with the singular subject twice over.
why.D: A plural auxiliary still fails to match the singular subject "archive".

context: Suppose the writer wanted to add a sentence stressing that the dialect boundary is not fixed. Which of the following would best accomplish that goal?

choices.text: The line has shifted twice since the first surveys, and no one expects it to hold.
The recordings are catalogued by date, by location and by the initials of the recordist.
A white-crowned sparrow weighs about as much as a small handful of paper clips.
Reel-to-reel tape was the standard recording medium throughout the 1960s.

why.A: Correct — a line that has already shifted twice is plainly not a fixed one.
why.B: Cataloguing practice says nothing about whether the boundary stays where it is.
why.C: The bird’s weight is a physical detail unrelated to where the two dialects meet.
why.D: The recording medium is background, and it leaves the boundary entirely unaddressed.

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to explain why a song can change faster than a beak can. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows the song is learned each generation while the body is not.
Yes, because it lists every location where the two dialects have been recorded.
No, because it never gives the shape or the size of the sparrow’s beak at all.
No, because it describes the recordings without saying who paid for them.

why.A: Correct — learning happens once a generation, while inheritance shifts far more slowly.
why.B: A list of locations would show where the dialects are, not why one can change quickly.
why.C: The beak is only an example of an inherited trait, so its measurements are beside the point.
why.D: Funding is irrelevant, and the essay does address how quickly a song can change.

context: The writer is considering deleting the statement that a male raised where he hears no adult singer invents a song of his own. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it shows that the song has to be learned from another bird.
Kept, because it names the month in which young males first begin to sing.
Deleted, because the essay is about boundaries rather than about single birds.
Deleted, because the opening paragraph has already made the same point.

why.A: Correct — the invented song is the evidence that learning, not instinct, supplies the tune.
why.B: No month appears anywhere in that statement, so the stated reason does not match it.
why.C: The single bird is exactly what explains how a boundary can move at all.
why.D: The opening paragraph describes the ridge and never mentions an isolated male.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence beginning "But the ridge itself is only a few hundred metres high" belongs:

choices.text: after the two slopes and their two songs have both been described.
at the very start of the essay, before either dialect is introduced.
in the final paragraph, after the account of how fast a song can change.
immediately before the explanation of how a young male learns his song.

why.A: Correct — the objection only lands once the reader knows a ridge divides the two.
why.B: Opening with an objection to a claim the reader has not yet met would only confuse.
why.C: By the final paragraph the ridge has dropped out of the discussion entirely.
why.D: The learning of the song is a separate thread, and the ridge interrupts it there.

context: The library, which had charged ten cents a day since «1971 stopped» charging anything in 2016.

why.A: A non-essential clause needs a comma at both ends, and the closing one is missing here.
why.B: Correct — the clause beginning "which" is fenced off by a comma at each end.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the left side is not one.
why.D: A colon delivers what an independent clause has promised, and none is promised here.

context: Since the amnesty took effect, circulation «has risen» in every branch but one.

why.A: Correct — "since" plus a result that still stands calls for the present perfect.
why.B: The past perfect would place the rise before some other past event, and none is given.
why.C: A simple past closes the rise off, but "since" keeps it running up to the present.
why.D: The present progressive drops the link back to the moment the amnesty took effect.

context: The staff «had expected in advance to anticipate» a wave of books that never came home.

why.A: "In advance" and "anticipate" both repeat what "expected" has already said.
why.B: Correct — one verb carries the whole meaning without saying it twice.
why.C: Anticipating is by definition done beforehand, so the phrase adds nothing at all.
why.D: Expecting also happens beforehand, which makes the added phrase redundant.

context: «Overdue for eleven years, a woman returned a field guide» in the second week.

choices.text: A woman returned a field guide that had been overdue for eleven years
Overdue for eleven years, the second week brought back a field guide
Returning a field guide, eleven years overdue was the woman

why.A: The opening phrase describes the field guide, but a woman is what follows the comma.
why.B: Correct — the eleven years attach to the guide, the only thing that was overdue.
why.C: This hands the overdue years to the second week, which cannot itself be overdue.
why.D: Inverting the clause leaves the phrase attached to nothing and the sentence unreadable.

context: The board’s first objection «, that the fines paid for something —» turned out to be the weaker one.

choices.text: — that the fines paid for something —
, that the fines paid for something;
: that the fines paid for something,

why.A: An interrupter has to open and close with the same mark, and a comma cannot close a dash.
why.B: Correct — the aside is fenced by a dash at each end, so the pair finally matches.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and neither side here is one.
why.D: A colon introduces what an independent clause has promised, which this aside is not.

context: The board asked the director and «I» to prepare a report on the first year.

why.A: The pronoun is the object of "asked", and "I" can only ever be a subject.
why.B: Correct — drop "the director and" and "asked me" is what remains.
why.C: A reflexive has to match the subject, and the board is the subject of this sentence.
why.D: "Mine" is a possessive form and cannot stand as the object of a verb.

context: Return rates barely moved. «Therefore,» the number of reinstated cards tripled in six months.

why.A: "Therefore" claims the flat return rate caused the tripling, which nothing supports.
why.B: Correct — the two facts run alongside each other, which is what "meanwhile" marks.
why.C: "Nevertheless" sets up a contrast, but neither fact works against the other one.
why.D: The reinstated cards are a second result rather than an instance of the return rate.

context: The report tracked how many books came back, how many cards were reopened, and «the rise in circulation».

why.A: A noun phrase breaks a series whose first two members are clauses beginning "how".
why.B: Correct — all three items now open with "how", so the series matches itself.
why.C: A gerund phrase is a third different shape, which leaves the list uneven.
why.D: An infinitive turns the third item into a purpose rather than a third thing tracked.

context: Neither the fine schedule nor the reminder letters «was» changed during the first year.

why.A: With "neither ... nor" the verb matches the nearer subject, and "letters" is plural.
why.B: Correct — "letters" sits closest to the verb, so the verb has to be plural.
why.C: This is singular as well as perfect, so it disagrees with the nearer subject.
why.D: A singular present-tense verb misses both the number and the past time frame.

context: The writer is considering adding a sentence naming the architecture firm that designed the library building. Should the sentence be added?

choices.text: No, because the essay is about the fines policy rather than the building.
No, because the firm is already named earlier in the same paragraph.
Yes, because it explains why the board was reluctant to lose the revenue.
Yes, because it shows that the library has served the city for a long time.

why.A: Correct — the architect has no bearing on what the fines did or on whom they fell.
why.B: No firm is named anywhere in the essay, so nothing would be repeated.
why.C: A design credit says nothing about revenue or about the board’s reasoning.
why.D: Length of service is not at issue, and the sentence would still change the subject.

context: The «librarians» objections were heard at three meetings before the vote.

why.A: With no apostrophe the word is a plain plural and shows no ownership at all.
why.B: Correct — several librarians own the objections, so the apostrophe follows the s.
why.C: The singular possessive would mean one librarian raised every objection.
why.D: A plural already ending in s never takes a second s after the apostrophe.

context: The amnesty had no «effect» on how quickly borrowed books came back.

why.A: Correct — the noun after "no" is "effect", and a result is exactly what is meant.
why.B: "Affect" is the verb form, and a verb cannot follow "no" in this position.
why.C: An affectation is a put-on manner, which has nothing to do with return times.
why.D: An -ing form cannot serve as the noun the sentence needs after "no".

context: Suppose the writer wanted to close the essay by stressing that the question is still open. Which of the following would best accomplish that goal?

choices.text: The board votes on the policy each year and has not yet voted the same way twice.
The library holds about four hundred thousand items across its seven branches.
Fines had been charged at ten cents a day without interruption since 1971.
The director keeps the first amnesty poster framed behind her office door.

why.A: Correct — a vote that keeps changing is the clearest sign the question is still open.
why.B: The size of the collection is a fact about the library, not about the argument.
why.C: The old fine rate is background and says nothing about what happens next.
why.D: A framed poster suggests the matter was closed, which is the opposite of the goal.

context: Three branches reported the same three problems«:» damaged spines, missing discs and unshelved returns.

why.A: Correct — an independent clause promises three problems, and a colon delivers the list.
why.B: A semicolon separates independent clauses, and a bare list of nouns is not one.

context: The reminder letters went out every Friday. «Although nobody on the staff expecting a reply.»

choices.text: Nobody on the staff expected a reply.
Although nobody on the staff expecting a reply,
Nobody on the staff, expecting a reply.

why.A: This has a subordinator and no finite verb, so it never becomes a sentence.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb turn the fragment into a real sentence.

context: My aunt Verity, who had worked the board for thirty-one «years kept» a clock in the same room.

why.A: A non-essential clause needs a comma at both ends, and the closing one is missing.
why.B: Correct — the clause beginning "who" is fenced off by a comma at each end.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the left side is not one.

context: The automatic equipment was «faster, nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise».

choices.text: faster; nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise
faster nobody in Ardnew has ever argued otherwise
faster, and nobody in Ardnew ever argued otherwise, either

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone make a comma splice.
why.B: Correct — a semicolon is strong enough to join two clauses that could each stand alone.

context: She let me plug the easy calls. «Although never the ones going out of the county.»

choices.text: She never let me plug the ones going out of the county.
Although never the ones going out of the county,
Never the ones going out of the county.

why.A: A subordinator with no subject and no finite verb cannot stand as a sentence.
why.B: Correct — a subject and a finite verb turn the fragment into a sentence.
why.C: A comma at the end leaves the clause subordinate and still dependent on something.
why.D: Dropping "although" removes the subordinator but supplies no verb, so it is still a fragment.

context: By the time the automatic equipment arrived, Verity «had worked» the board for thirty-one years.

why.A: Correct — the past perfect places the thirty-one years before the equipment arrived.
why.B: The present perfect runs up to now, but the arrival is finished and in the past.
why.C: A present-tense verb puts the work in the reader’s own time rather than in the past.

context: The row of small hinged shutters «drop» open whenever anyone lifts a receiver.

why.A: The subject is "row", which is singular; "of shutters" cannot change its number.
why.B: Correct — a singular subject takes the singular verb "drops".
why.C: This is plural as well as perfect, so it matches neither the subject nor the time frame.
why.D: A plural progressive still fails to agree with the singular subject "row".

context: Verity apologised to the man on the line for «myself» and then took the cord back.

why.A: A reflexive has to match the subject, and Verity rather than the narrator is the subject.
why.B: Correct — the object of "for" is the plain object pronoun.
why.C: "I" is a subject form and cannot follow a preposition.
why.D: "My" is possessive and needs a noun after it, which the sentence does not supply.

context: The «Cassidys» telephone rang at half past six on a morning in August.

why.A: Without an apostrophe the word is a plain plural and marks no ownership.
why.B: Correct — the family is plural and already ends in s, so the apostrophe follows it.

context: «Hanging on their weighted pulleys, I could see the cords» from the doorway.

choices.text: I could see the cords hanging on their weighted pulleys
Hanging on their weighted pulleys, the doorway showed the cords
The cords, I could see hanging on their weighted pulleys,
