why.B: Correct — the phrase now sits beside the cords, which are the things hanging.
why.C: This hands the pulleys to the doorway, which is not hanging from anything.

context: Verity knew the hours, knew the names, and «was aware of every routine» in Ardnew.

choices.text: the routines were known to her

why.A: The first two items share the verb "knew", so a different verb breaks the pattern.

context: The new equipment connected a call in under a second. «Likewise,» it knew nothing about the town.

why.A: "Likewise" claims the two sentences agree, and the second one takes something back.

context: The board held a hundred jacks «— one for every line in Ardnew —» and a hundred cords.

choices.text: — one for every line in Ardnew,

why.A: Correct — a pair of dashes fences off the aside with the same mark at each end.
why.B: An interrupter cannot open with a dash and close with a comma; the marks must match.

why.D: Semicolons separate independent clauses and cannot fence off a phrase like this.

context: The job came down to one thing that no wire carried«,» knowing the town.

why.A: A comma is too weak to deliver the thing the clause has just promised to name.
why.B: Correct — a colon introduces what an independent clause has announced is coming.
why.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and "knowing the town" is not one.
why.D: "That is" needs punctuation of its own and still leaves the introduction undone.

context: Verity was never impatient «of» a caller who could not remember a number.

why.A: "Impatient of" is used for things one refuses to tolerate, not for people one waits on.

context: The shutter dropped and «made an audible clicking sound that could be heard» in the kitchen.

why.A: "Audible" and "could be heard" say the same thing twice over in one phrase.
why.B: Correct — one plain verb carries the meaning and names the noise exactly.
why.C: "Sounded" drops the particular noise the shutter makes, which is the point of the line.
why.D: "Emitted a sound" is both longer and vaguer than the verb the sentence wants.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence beginning "None of that was written anywhere" belongs:

choices.text: after the list of what Verity knew about the town.
in the opening paragraph, before the board is described.
in the final paragraph, after the clock is mentioned.
before the sentence explaining that the narrator was thirteen.

why.A: Correct — "that" has nothing to point back to until the list of what she knew has run.

context: Suppose the writer wanted to add a sentence stressing how little public recognition the job carries. Which of the following would best accomplish that goal?

context: Suppose the writer’s goal had been to explain why technical accuracy is not enough in this craft. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

context: The writer is considering deleting the statement that the cast listens for a week without trying to imitate anything. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it is the step that makes the imitation come out right.
Kept, because it names the recordings Fennelly plays to her casts.
Deleted, because the essay is about accents rather than about rehearsal.
Deleted, because the paragraph has already described her method in full.

why.A: Correct — the next sentence says imitation goes wrong when it starts early.
why.B: No particular recording is named there, so the stated reason does not match.
why.C: Rehearsal is where the accent is built, so the two cannot be separated.
why.D: The sentence is the method; without it the paragraph describes nothing in particular.

context: The writer is considering adding a sentence listing the awards given each year for stage design and lighting. Should the sentence be added?

choices.text: No, because the essay is about a job that those lists leave out.
No, because stage design has already been discussed in an earlier paragraph.

why.C: Recognition of other crafts is a separate subject and not what the paragraph is about.
why.D: Her refusals turn on flattering the audience and have no bearing on any award.

context: Broadcasters’ speech has been «sanded down» by years of professional work.

context: Fennelly «refutes» the request whenever a director asks for a thicker accent.

why.B: Correct — "declines" is the plain verb for turning down something that was asked.
why.C: "Rebukes" is aimed at a person for wrongdoing, not at a request.
why.D: "Renounces" means giving up something one already holds or believes.

context: Ita Fennelly, who has coached in three «countries holds» that the job is misnamed.

why.A: A non-essential clause needs a comma at both ends, and the closing one is missing.

why.D: A colon delivers what a full clause has promised, and nothing has been promised.

context: Before she took her first coaching job, Fennelly «had studied» phonetics for four years.

context: «Sitting at the side of the rehearsal room, the notebook records» every vowel that slips.

context: Each of the three directors had «their» own reason for wanting the accent thickened.

why.A: "Each" is singular, so a plural pronoun does not agree with it in formal usage.

context: The vowel chart can be learned in a week. «Similarly, the habits» behind it take much longer.

context: She listens for where the weight falls, how long a pause runs, and «which consonants get dropped».

context: A «coachs» credit appears in six-point type on the last page of the programme.

context: For the sake of logic and coherence, the sentence "None of that survives in a photograph." belongs:

context: He «came to the realization that he had learned» the consistency by ruining things.

context: Pryce will not say why the badgers went «— that is somebody else’s work —» and he says so early.

why.A: Correct — paired dashes can enclose a full clause dropped into another sentence.
